Tischler and Piet Maes The citation for this ICTV Report chapter is the summary published as: Bradfute, S. B., Calisher, C. H., Klempa, B., Klingström, J., Kuhn, J. H., Laenen, L., Tischler, N. D., & Maes, P. (2024). ICTV Virus Taxonomy Profile: Hantaviridae 2024, Journal of General Virology 105, 001975 Corresponding author: Piet Maes ( [email protected] ) Edited by: Holly Hughes and Evelien Adriaenssens Posted: March 2024, updated June 2024 Summary Hantaviridae is a family for negative-sense RNA viruses with genomes of about 10.5–14.6 kb (Table 1 Hantaviridae ). The family includes eight genera ( Actinovirus and Percilovirus (subfamily Actantavirinae ), Agnathovirus (subfamily Agantavirinae ), Loanvirus , Mobatvirus , Orthohantavirus and Thottimvirus (subfamily Mammantavirinae ), and Reptillovirus (subfamily Repantavirinae ). These viruses are maintained in and/or transmitted by small mammals, but also by fish and reptiles. Several orthohantaviruses can infect humans, causing mild, severe, and sometimes-fatal diseases. Hantavirids produce enveloped virions containing three single-stranded RNA segments with open reading frames (ORFs) that encode a nucleoprotein (N), a glycoprotein precursor (GPC), and large (L) protein containing an RNA-directed RNA polymerase (RdRP) domain. Table 1 Hantaviridae. Characteristics of members of the family Hantaviridae. Characteristic Description* Example Hantaan virus (S segment: M14626; M segment: M14627; L segment: X55901), species Orthohantavirus hantanense Virion Enveloped, pleomorphic virions 80–160 nm in diameter with heterodimeric surface spikes Genome Three single-stranded RNA molecules (segments): small (S; 1.0–3.0 kb), medium (M; 3.4–4.8 kb), and large (L; 5.3–6.8 kb) Replication Ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes containing anti-genomic RNA serve as coding templates for synthesis of genomic RNA Translation Proteins are produced from capped and non-polyadenylated mRNAs. The 5′-cap structure is obtained via cap-snatching from cellular mRNAs Host range Fish (actinoviruses, agnathoviruses, perciloviruses), mammals (orthohantaviruses), and reptiles (reptilloviruses) Taxonomy Realm Riboviria , kingdom Orthornavirae , phylum Negarnaviricota , class Bunyaviricetes , order Elliovirales ; the family includes four subfamilies, eight genera, and 55 species * mostly based on experiments with mammalian orthohantaviruses Viruses assigned to each of the seven genera form genus-specifc monophyletic clades based on phylogenetic analysis of concatenated L protein/RdRP, glycoprotein and N sequences. Viruses from all seven genera share one or more of the following characteristics: (i) enveloped pleomorphic virions; (ii) tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA genome without polyadenylated tracts at the 3′-end; (iii) genomic sequence complementarity at the 5′- and 3′-ends; and (iv) capped but not polyadenylated virus mRNAs ( Maes et al., 2004 ). Piscine Hosts Genus Actinovirus . Viruses in this genus infect actinopterygian (percid, ogcocephalid, and triacanthodid, and possibly goblid and melanotaeniid) fish. Genus Agnathovirus . Viruses in this genus infect agnathan (myxinid) fish. Genus Percilovirus . Viruses in this genus infect actinopterygian ( gobiid, lophiid ) fish. Mammalian Hosts Genus Loanvirus. Viruses in this genus infect rhinolophid, verspertillionid, and possibly nycterid bats and possibly murid rodents. Genus Mobatvirus. Viruses in this genus infect emballonurid, hipposiderid, pteropodid and possibly molossid, and vespertillionid bats and soricid and talpid eulipotyphla. Genus Orthohantavirus. Viruses assigned to this genus infect soricid and talpid eulipotyphla and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents. Genus Thottimvirus. Viruses in this genus infect soricid and possibly talpid eulipotyphla. Reptilian Hosts Genus Reptillovirus . Viruses in this genus infect gekkonid and possibly scincid reptiles. Virion Morphology Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Physicochemical and physical properties Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Nucleic acid Hantavirids have tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA genomes (S, M, and L segments). The viral mRNAs are not polyadenylated and contain a 5′-methylated cap and several non-templated nucleotides at the 5′-end that are derived from host cell mRNAs via cap snatching ( Schmaljohn et al., 1985 , Jonsson and Schmaljohn 2001 , Vaheri et al., 2013 ). Further information is only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Proteins Hantavirids typically express three structural proteins. The most abundant structural protein in a hantavirion is N, which encapsidates the hantaviral genomic segments. The least abundant protein is L, which mediates viral genome replication and transcription. Two glycoprotein subunits, G N and G C , are produced from GPC and mediate entry of hantavirions ( Schmaljohn et al., 1985 , Spiropoulou 2001 , Vaheri et al., 2013 ). Specifics are only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Lipids Not reported but are likely derived from the Golgi apparatus and/or the host cell plasma membrane and therefore likely composed of phospholipids, glycolipids, fatty acids, and sterols. Carbohydrates Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Genome organization and replication S RNA encodes N and in some viruses NSs ( Jääskeläinen et al., 2007 , Vera-Otarola et al., 2012 ), M RNA encodes GPC, and the L RNA encodes L with its RdRP, helicase, and endonuclease domains ( Jonsson and Schmaljohn 2001 ) (Figure 1 Hantaviridae ). Specifics are only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Figure 1 Hantaviridae . Genome organization of representative hantaviruses. The 5′- and 3′- ends of all segments are complementary at their termini, likely promoting the formation of panhandle RNP complexes within the virion . GPC , glycoprotein precursor gene; L , large (protein) gene; N , nucleoprotein gene. Biology Hantavirids have been found in actinopterygian (gobiid, lophiid, percid, ogcocephalid, and triacanthodid, and possibly goblid and melanotaeniid) and agnathan (myxinid) fish; in emballonurid, hipposiderid, pteropodid, rhinolophid, verspertillionid, and possibly molossid and nycterid bats; in soricid and talpid eulipotyphla; in muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents; in gekkonid and possibly scincid reptiles; and potentially in coleopteran and plectopteran insects (see genus pages for details). Only orthohantaviruses are known to cause diseases (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Antigenicity Systematic antigenicity studies have only been reported for orthohantaviruses (see Orthohantavirus genus page). species demarcation criteria The availability of at least coding-complete sequences of all three genome segments may be sufficient for hantavirid classification in the absence of a cultured isolate. Demarcation of genera is based upon DivErsity pArtitioning by hieRarchical Clustering (DEmARC) analysis) using concatenated deduced S, M, and L segment expression product sequences ( Hantaviridae: current classification and future perspectives, Viruses, 11, 9, e0788">Laenen et al., 2019 ). DEmARC analysis gave a frequency distribution of Pairwise Evolutionary Distance (PED) values of which the threshold of 0.1 gave an optimal clustering cost of zero and is used as the hantavirid species demarcation criterium. Genera are demarked by a PED-value threshold of 0.95 and subfamilies are demarcated based on their distinct clustering in a Bayesian maximum clade credibility tree and a PED-value threshold of 3.5. Relationships within the family Phylogenetic relationships across the family have been estimated using Bayesian maximum clade credibility trees generated from complete N, GPC, and L amino-acid sequences; similar topologies are obtained with concatenated N and GPC sequences (Figure 2 Hantaviridae ). Figure 2 Hantaviridae . Maximum likelihood phylogenetic tree inferred using IQ-TREE. The tree was constructed based on 53 concatenated S and M segment (amino acid) sequences using the LG+R9 model of sequence evolution. Branch lengths represent the estimated number of substitutions per site. Bootstrap support values (>70%) are indicated at nodes, reflecting the degree of confidence in the branching pattern. Relationships with other taxa Hantavirids are closely related to bunyaviral crulivirids, fimovirids, peribunyavirids, phasmavirids, tulasvirids, and tospovirids ( Wolf et al., 2018 , Herath et al., 2020 ). Using the Master Species List Using the Virus Metadata Resource Using the Find the Species tool Using the ICTV Report Webinar Webinar on Virus Taxonomy Webinar on Finding Information GitHub Repository Zenodo Repository Email ICTV Help ‏‏‎ ‎ ICTV Report Book: Hantaviridae Family: Hantaviridae Subfamily: Actantavirinae Genus: Actinovirus Genus: Percilovirus Subfamily: Agantavirinae Genus: Agnathovirus Subfamily: Mammantavirinae Genus: Loanvirus Genus: Mobatvirus Genus: Orthohantavirus Genus: Thottimvirus Subfamily: Repantavirinae Genus: Reptillovirus Authors: Hantaviridae Citation: Hantaviridae References: Hantaviridae Resources: Hantaviridae Species List: Hantaviridae Subfamily: Mammantavirinae Genus: Orthohantavirus Distinguishing features Sixty different viruses are classified in the genus Orthohantavius. These viruses typically infect specific soricid and talpid eulipotyphla and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents. Orthohantaviruses are the only hantavirids known to cause disease in humans ( Schmaljohn and Hjelle 1997 , Jonsson et al., 2010 , Kuhn and Schmaljohn 2023 , Vial et al., 2023 ). Virion Morphology Orthohantavirions are pleomorphic in shape, mostly spherical of 80–160 nm in diameter ( Huiskonen et al., 2010 ), and surrounded by a membrane envelope that is decorated with glycoprotein (GP) spikes composed of G N and G C subunits (Figure 1 Orthohantavirus ). The virion envelope is 5 nm thick and is decorated with square shaped spikes, consisting of tetrameric G N -G C heterodimers, which protrude 10 nM from the membrane forming a surface lattice of local symmetry interrupted by empty membrane spots ( Hung et al., 1983 , Huiskonen et al., 2010 , Battisti et al., 2011 , Parvate et al., 2019 , Serris et al., 2020 , Guardado-Calvo and Rey 2021 ). Isolated ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes are composed of individual segment genomic RNA encapsidated by nucleoprotein (N) ( Tao et al., 1987 , Huiskonen et al., 2010 , Battisti et al., 2011 , Hepojoki et al., 2012 , Guo et al., 2016 , Arragain et al., 2019 ). Virions assemble and bud from the Golgi complex or cell surface membranes, depending on the virus ( Goldsmith et al., 1995 , Parvate et al., 2019 ). Figure 1 Orthohantavirus. A, B) Electron micrographs of Tula virus particles adapted from ( Huiskonen et al., 2010 ). C) Schematic illustration of an orthohantavirus particle. Shown is a spherical and enveloped (grey) particle with glycoprotein spikes (G N yellow, G C blue) inserted in a bilaminar lipid envelope. The S (small), M (medium), and L (large) RNP (ribonucleoprotein) complexes inside the particle consist of N (nucleoprotein, green) and L (large protein, pink). ViralZone image reproduced courtesy of SwissBioPics. Physicochemical and physical properties Virion buoyant densities in sucrose and CsCl are 1.15–1.18 ( White et al., 1982 ) and 1.20–1.21 g cm −3 , respectively ( Schmaljohn et al., 1983 ). Virions are sensitive to chemical inactivation with, for instance, methanol, paraformaldehyde, acetone/methanol, N -ethylmaleimide or detergents, as well as physical methods such as heat, gamma irradiation or UV irradiation ( Kraus et al., 2005 , Strandin et al., 2011 , Elveborg et al., 2022 ). Nucleic acid Orthohantavirus genomes are linear tri-segmented RNA molecules of negative polarity. The genomes are about 11.1–12.3 kb in length (small [S] segment: 1.2–2.1 kb; medium [M] segment: 3.4–3.8 kb; large [L] segment: 6.5–6.6 kb). Proteins Orthohantaviruses typically express three structural proteins (Table 1 Orthohantavirus ). The most abundant structural protein in an orthohantavirion is N, which encapsidates the orthohantaviral genomic segments. The least abundant protein is L, which mediates viral genome replication and transcription. Two glycoprotein subunits, G N and G C , mediate virion entry. G N and G C and non-structural proteins are encoded as a precursor polyprotein. Table 1 Orthohantavirus . Location and function of orthohantavirus structural proteins. Protein Location, mass, and function Reference Nucleoprotein (N) Structural virion protein (about 48 kD). Oligomerizes and encapsidates orthohantaviral genomic segments and hence component of RNPs. Binds to L and G N ( Mir et al., 2010 , Reuter and Krüger 2018 , Arragain et al., 2019 ) Nonstructural protein (NSs) Non-structural protein encoded by some orhtohantaviruses. Has type I interferon inhibitory activity. May occur as multiple isoforms. ( Vera-Otarola et al., 2020 , Binder et al., 2021 ) Glycoprotein (GP) Structural virion protein consisting of two subunits (G N : about 70-75 kD, G C : about 50-55 kD). Produced via proteolytic cleavage from the genome-encoded precursor GPC. Projects from virion membranes as tetrameric GP spikes composed of G N and G C heterodimers. GP mediates cell- receptor binding; as a class II fusion machine it induces virion-cell membrane fusion and, thereby cell entry. G N binds to N and RNA ( Spiropoulou et al., 2003 , Tischler et al., 2005 , Cifuentes-Muñoz et al., 2014 , Li et al., 2016 , Willensky et al., 2016 , Rissanen et al., 2017 , Zhu et al., 2018 , Bignon et al., 2019 , Sperber et al., 2019 ) Large protein (L) Structural virion protein (246 kD) with RdRP, helicase, and endoribonuclease domains. Component of the RNP inside virions. Binds to N and RNA. Oligomerizes and mediates transcription and replication of viral RNA segments. Mediates cap-snatching for viral mRNA capping. ( Kukkonen et al., 2005 , Cheng et al., 2014 , Rothenberger et al., 2016 , Jeeva et al., 2019 , Durieux Trouilleton et al., 2023 ) Genome organization and replication The orthohantavirus genome consists of three negative-sense RNA molecules, termed S (small), M (medium), and L (large) (Figure 2 Orthohantavirus ). Figure 2 Orthohantavirus. Schematic representation of orthohantavirus genome organization. Orthohantavirus genomic segments assume circular forms via non-covalent binding of complementary and highly conserved 3′- and 5′-terminal sequences. Genomic segment reassortment mostly occurs among viruses belonging to the same species but interspecies reassortment likely occurs occasionally ( Klempa 2018 , Petazzi et al., 2021 ). Orthohantavirus infection starts with virion attachment, mediated by G N and G C , to cell-surface attachment factors and entry via the endosomal route ( Shtanko et al., 2014 ) (Figure 3 Orthohantavirus ). Figure 3 Orthohantavirus . Lifecycle of orthohantaviruses. (1) Virion attachment; (2) virion uptake; (3) virion-cell membrane fusion; (4) transcription; (5) translation; (6) replication; (7) virion assembly; and (8) virion egress. After engaging a cellular receptor, protocadherin 1 in the case of American orthohantaviruses, virion-membrane fusion results in early or late endosomal release, depending on the virus, of the virion RNP complex into the cytoplasm in a pH-dependent manner ( Jangra et al., 2018 , Mittler et al., 2019 , Torriani et al., 2019 , Dieterle et al., 2021 ). During primary transcription L generates uncapped antigenomic RNA molecules that are then capped using host cell-derived capped primers (cap snatching). L and S segment-transcribed mRNAs are translated by free ribosomes ( Garcin et al., 1995 , Jeeva et al., 2019 , Meier et al., 2021 ). M segment-transcribed mRNA is translated by membrane-bound ribosomes, with the expressed GPC which is likely co-translationally cleaved by cellular proteases to yield G N and G C . The synthesis of the antigenome by L protein serves as a template for genomic RNA replication. Secondary transcription amplifies the synthesis of mRNAs and genome replication. During morphogenesis, G N and G C accumulate in the Golgi apparatus, modified host membranes are acquired, and virions bud into the Golgi. Biology Genus Orthohantavirus includes 38 species for 60 distinct viruses. These viruses and their unclassified, potential relatives, subclinically, and often chronically, infect specific soricid and talpid eulipotyphla, and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents ( Jonsson et al., 2010 , Wu et al., 2018 , Chen et al., 2023 , Kuhn and Schmaljohn 2023 ). Orthohantaviruses are overall distributed worldwide, but the individual geographic distribution is dependent on host range. At least some orthohantaviruses may not be as restricted to a particular host as originally thought, but may be carried by animals of multiple hosts ( Goodfellow et al., 2021 , Quizon et al., 2022 , Gu et al., 2023 ). Orthohantaviruses are the only hantavirids known to cause disease (all in humans) and all disease-causing viruses are rodent-borne. Human infection may occur after inhalation of aerosolized excreta or secreta of infected rodents or direct rodent contact. The two WHO-recognized orthohantavirus-caused diseases are hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), caused by Asian and European viruses (in particular Dobrava virus [DOBV], Hantaan virus [HTNV], Puumala virus [PUUV] and Seoul virus [SEOV]), and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), a frequently lethal disease caused by viruses from the Americas (in particular Andes virus [ANDV] and Sin Nombre virus [SNV]) ( Vial et al., 2023 ). The hamster model of wild-type ANDV infection is lethal and largely mimics human HPS ( Hooper et al., 2001 ). After SNV infection in nonhuman primates, some animals develop an HPS-like disease, but cell passage of SNV can result in mutations that render the virus non-pathogenic in this model ( Safronetz et al., 2014 ). Many rodent models result in a chronic, asymptomatic infection, and these have been used in early-stage therapeutic studies ( Strandin et al., 2020 ). However, recent advances have been made in development of an HFRS mouse model using HTNV variants ( Wei et al., 2022 ). Orthohantavirus animal models are reviewed in ( Golden et al., 2015 ). Antigenicity There is considerable serum cross-reactivity between the nucleocapsids of hantavirids, but neutralizing antibodies targeting Gn/Gc are more specific. SNV was first identified as a hantavirid based on cross-reactivity of patient sera with other orthohantavirus antigens ( 1993 ). Similarly, rodents that carried SNV were identified in serosurveys using non-SNV orthohantavirus antigens, since SNV had not been isolated at the time ( Childs et al., 1994 ). Species demarcation criteria Demarcation of species is based upon DivErsity pArtitioning by hieRarchical Clustering (DEmARC) analysis) using concatenated deduced S, M, and L segment expression product sequences ( Laenen et al., 2019 ). Phylogenetic relationships across the genus have been estimated using maximum likelihood trees generated from complete N, GPC and L amino-acid sequences, and for N and GPC amino-acid sequences (Figure 2 Hantaviridae ). Hantaviridae ~ ViralZone Skip to main content ViralZone Hantaviridae (taxid:1980413) VIRION Enveloped, spherical. Diameter from 80 to 120nm. GENOME Segmented Negative-stranded RNA linear genome, L segment is between 6.8 and 12 kb, M segment between 3.2 and 4.9 kb and S segment between 1 and 3 kb. Encodes for four to six proteins. Some hantaviruses also encode a NSs protein on their S segment. GENE EXPRESSION The viral RNA dependent RNA polymerase (L) binds to a promoter on each encapsidated segment, and transcribes the mRNA. These are capped by L protein during synthesis using cap snatching . Transcription is terminated by a strong hairpin sequence at the end of each gene. Puumala virus expressed an additional NSs by leaky scanning in the NS gene. ENZYMES RNA-dependent RNA polymerase L Cap Snatching endonuclease L REPLICATION CYTOPLASMIC Virus attaches to host receptors though Gn-Gc glycoprotein dimer, and is endocytosed into vesicles in the host cell. Fusion of virus membrane with the vesicle membrane; ribonucleocapsid segments are released in the cytoplasm. Transcription , viral mRNAs are capped in the cytoplasm. Replication presumably starts when enough nucleoprotein is present to encapsidate neo-synthetized antigenomes and genomes. The ribonucleocapsids buds at Golgi apparatus, releasing the virion by exocytosis. The hantaviruses (Hantaviridae) ~ ViralZone Skip to main content ViralZone Back to Andes virus resource There are approximately 92 known viruses in the family Hantaviridae, classified into 52 species. Each species is typically adapted to a specific reservoir host, most commonly rodents, but also bats and moles. With the notable exception of Andes virus, hantaviruses are generally not transmitted from person to person. Based on their geographic distribution, evolutionary relationships, and the diseases they cause in humans, hantaviruses can be broadly divided into three major groups: New World hantaviruses (the Americas) These viruses cause Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), a severe respiratory disease. Important examples include Sin Nombre virus and Andes virus. Annual incidence are about 100 cases per year (Andes virus) about 25 cases per year (Sin Nombre virus) Old World hantaviruses (Asia) These viruses are responsible for Hantavirus hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), which is characterized by fever, hemorrhage, and acute kidney injury. Major examples include Hantaan virus and Seoul virus. Annual incidence: more than 10,000 cases worldwide Old World hantaviruses (Europe) European hantaviruses typically cause a milder form of HFRS known as Nephropathia epidemica (NE). The main causative agents are Puumala virus and Dobrava-Belgrade virus. Annual incidence: more than 1,000 cases Together, these viruses represent an important and diverse group of zoonotic pathogens that can cause severe disease following accidental transmission from their natural animal hosts to humans.

papers.title: Expanded protocadherin-1 usage reveals a broader hantavirus entry landscape.
papers.abstract: Mammalian hantaviruses are RNA viruses that cause hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome in the Americas and hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome in Eurasia. The cellular entry mechanisms of most hantaviruses remain poorly defined. To examine entry by phylogenetically distinct hantaviruses identified across Africa, Eurasia, and the Americas, we generated replication-competent recombinant vesicular stomatitis viruses (rVSVs) bearing Gn/Gc proteins from Necoclí, Sangassou, Thottapalayam, Kenkeme, Nova, Oxbow, and Tula viruses. All these Gn/Gc proteins except Kenkeme supported infection of primary human endothelial cells, indicating that endothelial cell entry is permissive for a broader range of hantaviruses than previously appreciated. Except for rVSV-Kenkeme, these rVSVs did not acquire additional mutations beyond pre-engineered rescue-enhancing changes during rescue and passaging. Genetic studies in human cells lacking protocadherin-1 (PCDH1) showed that Necoclí, Tula, and Nova viruses use PCDH1 for efficient infection, although the Nova phenotype was weaker. These three Gn/Gc proteins bound soluble PCDH1 with different apparent avidities, and infection by the corresponding rVSVs was inhibited by soluble PCDH1; Necoclí and Tula, but not Nova, were also blocked by a PCDH1-targeting monoclonal antibody. Authentic Tula virus infection was similarly reduced in PCDH1 knockout endothelial cells. Finally, the broadly reactive anti-Gn/Gc human monoclonal antibody ADI-42898 efficiently neutralized Necoclí, Nova, Sangassou, and Kenkeme rVSVs, but showed weak or undetectable activity against Oxbow, Tula, and Thottapalayam rVSVs. Together, these findings expand the range of hantavirus glycoproteins capable of mediating infection of human endothelial cells, broaden the phylogenetic scope of PCDH1-dependent entry, and identify receptor-targeted and viral glycoprotein-targeted strategies with differential activity.IMPORTANCEMany newly discovered hantaviruses are known only from sequence data, leaving their ability to enter human cells and their receptor usage unresolved. Using a BSL2-compatible recombinant vesicular stomatitis virus (rVSV) system, we show that glycoproteins from several divergent hantaviruses can mediate infection of primary human endothelial cells, indicating that endothelial cell entry is permissive for a broader range of hantaviruses than previously appreciated. We also show that protocadherin-1 (PCDH1), previously linked mainly to New World hantaviruses, is used by Necoclí, Tula, and Nova viruses but not universally across the panel, revealing broader but heterogeneous receptor usage. An authentic Tula virus experiment supports this conclusion beyond the surrogate system. Finally, a broadly reactive anti-Gn/Gc antibody neutralizes several, but not all, of these viruses, highlighting both the promise and the limits of broadly protective countermeasures and the utility of these rVSVs for evaluating entry inhibitors.

analysis.methods: The study generated replication‑competent recombinant vesicular stomatitis viruses (rVSVs) bearing Gn/Gc proteins from seven diverse hantaviruses and evaluated infection of primary human endothelial cells, including PCDH1‑knockout cells, with additional soluble‑PCDH1 binding and neutralization assays.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Mammalian hantaviruses cause severe disease, but most entry mechanisms are unknown. Methods: Researchers used rVSVs with diverse hantavirus Gn/Gc proteins to infect primary human endothelial cells, including PCDH1‑knockout cells, and performed binding and neutralization assays. Results: All Gn/Gc except Kenkeme infected cells; Necoclí, Tula, and Nova required PCDH1 (Nova weaker); soluble PCDH1 and a monoclonal antibody blocked entry; authentic Tula infection was reduced in PCDH1‑KO cells; a broad anti‑Gn/Gc antibody neutralized several but not all viruses. Contribution: The work broadens the known hantavirus entry landscape, reveals heterogeneous PCDH1 usage, and highlights targeted therapeutic strategies. Limitations: not reported in the supplied evidence.

papers.title_zh: 扩展的protocadherin-1利用揭示了更广泛的 汉坦病毒 进入格局。

analysis_zh.background: 哺乳动物 汉坦病毒 是RNA病毒,可在美洲导致 汉坦病毒心肺综合征,在欧亚地区导致 肾综合征出血热,但大多数 汉坦病毒 的细胞进入机制仍未明确。
analysis_zh.methods: 本研究构建了携带七种不同 汉坦病毒 Gn/Gc 蛋白的可复制重组水疱性口炎病毒 (rVSV),并评估其对原代人类内皮细胞(包括 PCDH1 基因敲除细胞)的感染,同时进行可溶性 PCDH1 结合和中和实验。
analysis_zh.results: 除 Kenkeme 外,所有 Gn/Gc 蛋白均可介导内皮细胞感染;Necoclí、Tula 和 Nova 病毒依赖 PCDH1 实现高效进入(Nova 较弱);可溶性 PCDH1 能结合这些糖蛋白并抑制感染;针对 PCDH1 的单克隆抗体阻断了 Necoclí 和 Tula;在 PCDH1‐KO 细胞中,真实的 Tula 感染被降低;抗 Gn/Gc 抗体 ADI‐42898 中和了多株 rVSV,但对其他株的活性弱或无效。
analysis_zh.contribution: 这些发现扩展了能够介导人类内皮细胞进入的 汉坦病毒 糖蛋白范围,扩大了 PCDH1 依赖性进入的系统发育范围,并确定了针对受体和糖蛋白的差异性活性策略,为潜在对策提供依据。
analysis_zh.limitations: 未在提供的证据中报告。

papers.title: Vascular Programs in Emerging and Re-Emerging RNA Virus Infections: Comparative Lessons from SARS-CoV-2, Flaviviruses, and Hantaviruses
papers.abstract: Emerging and re-emerging RNA viruses frequently present with clinical phenotypes that extend beyond classical organ tropism and include vascular leakage, platelet dysregulation, coagulation imbalance, microvascular injury, and thromboinflammation. SARS-CoV-2, flaviviruses, and hantaviruses provide three complementary models of virus-induced vascular disease. This narrative review compares these viruses through a shared endothelial–coagulative framework and proposes four partially overlapping vascular programs: endothelial activation, endothelial barrier failure, coagulation activation, and platelet quantitative or qualitative dysfunction. These programs are intended as a conceptual synthesis of convergent clinical, pathological, and experimental evidence rather than as a quantitative classification system. The framework is used not only to organize known mechanisms, but also to generate testable predictions for cross-virus biomarker panels, organ-specific endothelial models, and phenotype-guided clinical studies. Severe COVID-19 illustrates inflammation-driven endothelial activation, platelet–leukocyte interactions, complement amplification, NETosis, and immunothrombosis. Within the flavivirus group, DENV is used as the principal model for systemic vascular leakage, thrombocytopenia, and hemorrhagic risk; selected non-dengue flaviviruses illustrate how shared endothelial, platelet, and coagulation modules are redirected toward placental dysfunction (ZIKV), neuroinvasion (WNV and JEV), or hepatic failure and coagulopathy (YFV). Hantavirus infections provide a distinctive model of capillary leak syndrome in which non-lytic endothelial infection, immune-mediated injury, and permeability signaling converge on renal and pulmonary microvascular beds. A comparative view suggests that thrombotic, hemorrhagic, and leaky phenotypes are not mutually exclusive categories, but different outcomes of overlapping vascular programs shaped by viral tropism, vascular-bed specialization, immune activation, and host susceptibility.

analysis.background: Emerging and re‑emerging RNA viruses often cause vascular pathology beyond their primary organ tropism, prompting a review of shared vascular mechanisms.
analysis.main_directions: The review uses SARS‑CoV‑2, flaviviruses, and hantaviruses as complementary models and frames virus‑induced vascular disease into four overlapping programs: endothelial activation, barrier failure, coagulation activation, and platelet dysfunction.
analysis.current_state: Current evidence shows inflammation‑driven endothelial activation and immunothrombosis in severe COVID‑19, systemic leakage and thrombocytopenia in dengue, organ‑specific vascular effects in other flaviviruses, and immune‑mediated capillary leak in hantavirus infection.
analysis.gaps: The proposed programs are a conceptual synthesis rather than a quantitative classification, leaving uncertainty about their precise boundaries and the relative contribution of each pathway across viruses.
analysis.future_research: The authors suggest generating cross‑virus biomarker panels, developing organ‑specific endothelial models, and conducting phenotype‑guided clinical studies to test the framework.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Emerging RNA viruses often cause vascular pathology beyond organ tropism. Main directions: SARS‑CoV‑2, flaviviruses, and hantaviruses illustrate four overlapping vascular programs (endothelial activation, barrier failure, coagulation activation, platelet dysfunction). Current state: Evidence links severe COVID‑19 to immunothrombosis, dengue to leakage and thrombocytopenia, other flaviviruses to organ‑specific vascular effects, and hantaviruses to immune‑mediated capillary leak. Gaps: The framework is conceptual, not quantitative, so pathway contributions remain uncertain. Future research: Develop cross‑virus biomarker panels, organ‑specific endothelial models, and phenotype‑guided clinical studies.

papers.title_zh: 新发与再发RNA病毒感染中的血管程序:来自SARS‐CoV‐2、黄病毒及汉坦病毒的比较经验

analysis_zh.background: 新发和再发RNA病毒常在其主要器官嗜性之外导致血管病理,促使对共享血管机制进行综述。
analysis_zh.main_directions: 本综述以SARS‐CoV‐2、黄病毒和汉坦病毒为互补模型,将病毒诱导的血管疾病划分为四个相互重叠的程序:内皮激活、屏障失效、凝血激活和血小板功能障碍。
analysis_zh.current_state: 现有证据显示,重症COVID‐19中炎症驱动的内皮激活和免疫血栓形成,登革热中全身渗漏和血小板减少,其他黄病毒中器官特异性血管效应,以及汉坦病毒感染中的免疫介导毛细血管漏出。
analysis_zh.gaps: 所提出的程序是一种概念性综合,而非定量分类,因而对其精确边界以及各病毒中各通路的相对贡献仍存不确定性。
analysis_zh.future_research: 作者建议构建跨病毒生物标志物面板,研发器官特异性内皮模型,并开展基于表型的临床研究以验证该框架。

papers.title: IDENTIFICATION OF A STRUCTURALLY AND EVOLUTIONARILY CONSERVED 3'→5' PROOFREADING EXONUCLEASE DOMAIN IN THE LARGE L PROTEIN OF HANTAVIRUSES- EMERGING HUMAN PATHOGENS
papers.abstract: The proofreading 3′→5′ exonuclease not only represents a crucial class of enzymes responsible for maintaining genome integrity across diverse groups of organisms, but also plays a critical role in ensuring replication fidelity. In the non-segmented, positive-strand bat-borne RNA viruses like Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronaviruses (SARS-CoVs and MERS-CoV), it is found along with the methyltransferase (MTase) gene of the non-structural protein 14 (NSP14). In contrast, in the non-segmented, but negative-strand bat-borne RNA viruses such as Marburg, Ebola and Nipah viruses, it has been identified together with a novel type of capping enzyme, viz. guanosine diphosphate polyribonucleotidyltransferase (PRNTase). Hantaviruses, one of the fatal and emerging human pathogens in recent times, belong to segmented, negative-strand RNA viruses and are primarily rodent-borne. Currently, no universally approved vaccine or antiviral therapy exists for all hantavirus infections. The presence of a proofreading (PR) exonuclease domain has not been reported in hantaviruses until now. Interestingly, a putative PR exonuclease domain has been identified for the first time in these viruses within the large L protein, preceding the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp). The newly identified domain belongs to the DEDD superfamily, but exhibits a distinct structural deviation, notably the replacement of the first catalytic triad -DxE- in the Old World hantaviruses with an -NxE- motif in most of the New World hantaviruses, and the use of an invariant tyrosine instead of histidine at the proton acceptor site. This feature closely resembles the DEDD superfamily of PR exonucleases reported in bacterial DNA polymerases I and II and in the DNA-dependent DNA polymerases of DNA viruses. To the best of my knowledge, this study provides the first evidence for the presence of a typical DEDD superfamily of PR exonuclease domain in hantaviruses, and thus, expanding our understanding of the structure and catalytic mechanism of 3′→5′ PR exonucleases in segmented, negative-strand RNA viruses and further presenting a novel structural target for the development of universally effective antiviral therapies against fatal hantavirus infections.
papers.journal: World Journal of Advanced Research and Reviews

source_records.title: IDENTIFICATION OF A STRUCTURALLY AND EVOLUTIONARILY CONSERVED 3'→5' PROOFREADING EXONUCLEASE DOMAIN IN THE LARGE L PROTEIN OF HANTAVIRUSES- EMERGING HUMAN PATHOGENS
source_records.abstract: The proofreading 3′→5′ exonuclease not only represents a crucial class of enzymes responsible for maintaining genome integrity across diverse groups of organisms, but also plays a critical role in ensuring replication fidelity. In the non-segmented, positive-strand bat-borne RNA viruses like Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronaviruses (SARS-CoVs and MERS-CoV), it is found along with the methyltransferase (MTase) gene of the non-structural protein 14 (NSP14). In contrast, in the non-segmented, but negative-strand bat-borne RNA viruses such as Marburg, Ebola and Nipah viruses, it has been identified together with a novel type of capping enzyme, viz. guanosine diphosphate polyribonucleotidyltransferase (PRNTase). Hantaviruses, one of the fatal and emerging human pathogens in recent times, belong to segmented, negative-strand RNA viruses and are primarily rodent-borne. Currently, no universally approved vaccine or antiviral therapy exists for all hantavirus infections. The presence of a proofreading (PR) exonuclease domain has not been reported in hantaviruses until now. Interestingly, a putative PR exonuclease domain has been identified for the first time in these viruses within the large L protein, preceding the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp). The newly identified domain belongs to the DEDD superfamily, but exhibits a distinct structural deviation, notably the replacement of the first catalytic triad -DxE- in the Old World hantaviruses with an -NxE- motif in most of the New World hantaviruses, and the use of an invariant tyrosine instead of histidine at the proton acceptor site. This feature closely resembles the DEDD superfamily of PR exonucleases reported in bacterial DNA polymerases I and II and in the DNA-dependent DNA polymerases of DNA viruses. To the best of my knowledge, this study provides the first evidence for the presence of a typical DEDD superfamily of PR exonuclease domain in hantaviruses, and thus, expanding our understanding of the structure and catalytic mechanism of 3′→5′ PR exonucleases in segmented, negative-strand RNA viruses and further presenting a novel structural target for the development of universally effective antiviral therapies against fatal hantavirus infections.

World Journal of Advanced Research and Reviews, 2026, 32(01), 969–979 970 1 INTRODUCTION Viruses are ubiquitous in nature, infecting and proliferating in organisms across all kingdoms of life. They have evolved and adapted their lifecycles to the organisms they infect and, following successful infection, viruses rely predominantly on their host’s cellular machinery for their survival and proliferation. Based on the nature of their genome, viruses are broadly classified into RNA and DNA viruses. Both types cause diseases in plants, animals and humans, ranging from endemic to pandemic proportions, resulting in major global healthcare crises and unprecedented economic losses, necessitating a deeper understanding of their pathogenic and replication mechanisms to develop effective therapeutic interventions [1]. However, the majority of the serious human diseases are caused by RNA viruses belonging to both negative- and positive-strand viruses [2]. For example, Measles, Mumps, Human influenza viruses (A, B and C), Hendra, Cedar, Ebola, Marburg, Nipah, Rabies, etc. are caused by the non-segmented, negative-strand RNA viruses whereas SARS-CoVs, MERS-CoV, Polio, Hepatitis C, Dengue, Zika, Yellow fever, Rubella, Encephalomyocarditis, HIVs, etc. belong to non-segmented, but positive-strand RNA viruses. Again, some of the RNA viruses possess segmented, single-stranded genomes like human influenza viruses (8 segments) and hantaviruses (3 segments), whereas some possess segmented, double-stranded RNA genomes like rotavirus and bluetongue virus. Hantaviruses are emerging human pathogens that cause severe, often fatal, hemorrhagic fevers and pulmonary syndromes. They have been responsible for several human disease outbreaks in recent years. Furthermore, human-to- human transmission in recent years has established hantaviruses as one of the most dangerous viruses [3, 4]. In fact, hantaviruses are more serious and lethal than the SARS-CoV-2, as some of them have a greater mortality rate (~50%) than the latter (~1% global average). Mostly hantaviruses are not transmitted between humans. However, the Andes orthohantavirus in South America has demonstrated limited person-to-person transmission, particularly among those in close contact. For example, recently, an outbreak of the Andes orthohantavirus on a cruise ship infected 11 people and killed three earlier this year (2026). Hantavirus was first discovered following the Korean War. During the war, haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) was a common ailment in soldiers stationed near the Hantan River. This illness is now considered as one of the most serious haemorrhagic diseases in the world, like Ebola haemorrhagic fever, due to its high mortality rate and epidemic potential. The first hantavirus was isolated in 1978 in South Korea and was named Hantaan virus. Based on the geographic distribution, hantaviruses are broadly classified into Old World hantaviruses, which typically cause HFRS and are prevalent in Africa, Asia, and Europe, (e.g., Hantaan virus, Seoul virus, Puumala virus, Dobrava-Belgrade virus, Amur virus, etc.) and New World hantaviruses (e.g., Andes virus, Sin Nombre virus, Laguna Negra virus, Black Creek Canal virus, Choclo virus, etc.) which are associated with hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) in the Americas [5, 6]. The hantaviruses are primarily rodent-borne and are the main source of human infections, although new hantaviruses have recently been reported or isolated from bats, moles and shrews [7, 8]. Spillover of these viruses to humans can result in one of the two serious illnesses. The case fatality rate of HFRS ranges from 1% to 15%, while for HPS, it is 30–60% [9]. Thus, both diseases can be fatal, but with differing mortality rates. Currently, there is neither an approved vaccine nor a specific and effective antiviral treatment available for human use. Importantly, hantaviruses can survive for 10 days at room temperature, 15 days in temperate environments and more than 18 days at 4 °C (39 °F), which facilitates their stable transmission [9, 10]. Therefore, understanding the structure of the hantavirus genome and the functions of the key viral proteins is critical for developing effective antiviral therapeutic agents to control the spread of the virus. 1.1 Classification of hantaviruses Hantaviruses belong to the genus Orthohantavirus and the order Bunyavirales within the family of Hantaviridae. They are enveloped, negative-sense, single-stranded RNA viruses that cause two potentially lethal zoonotic syndromes, viz. HFRS and HPS as discussed elsewhere. It is estimated that, globally, around 1.5 million people get infected with hantaviruses each year with typical case fatality rates of up to 15 % for HFRS and around 40 % or higher for HPS [11]. Hantaviruses are further classified into Old World (HFRS-causing) and New World (HPS-causing) viruses [3]. The Old World hantaviruses are primarily found in Europe and Asia and typically cause HFRS with a mortality rate of up to 15%. Examples include, Hantaan virus, Seoul virus, Puumala virus, Dobrava-Belgrade virus, Amur virus, etc. The New World hantaviruses are more dangerous and prevalent in North and South America and are associated with HPS with mortality rates reaching up to 40%. Examples include, Sin Nombre virus, Andes virus, Laguna Negra virus, Black Creek Canal virus. Choclo virus, etc. [12]. Among the hantaviruses, only the New World Andes virus has been demonstrated to have the potential for human-to-human transmission [4]. 1.2 3’→5’ PR exonucleases and their classifications PR exonucleases (EC 3.1.11.x) are ubiquitous enzymes that play a crucial role in repairing error(s) during replication of genomes and thus, maintain the integrity of genomes in organisms. They remove misincorporated wrong nucleotides in the 3′→ 5′ direction during DNA/RNA synthesis. Based on their conserved active site amino acids, these enzymes are broadly classified into two superfamilies, viz. the DEDD and the Polymerase and Histidinol Phosphatase (PHP) superfamilies [13, 14]. The DEDD superfamily is the most common type of PR enzyme and is reported from both DNA World Journal of Advanced Research and Reviews, 2026, 32(01), 969–979 971 and RNA polymerases from a large number of organisms from viruses to humans. The name derives from the four highly conserved acidic amino acid residues, viz. DEDD, in its active site for metal-binding and catalysis. The PHP superfamily, characterized by the active site amino acid structure, HxH-E-H-D, uses His residues for metal-binding and catalysis. Bacterial/Archaeal DNA polymerases X, bacterial DNA polymerases III (bacterial replicases) with a co-editing, built-in exonuclease [14, 15] and YcdX phosphoesterases [16] belong to PHP superfamily. Both superfamilies are essentially Zn- dependent enzymes and initiate the catalysis from a metal-bound water molecule [17]. It is interesting to note that certain viruses like the human influenza viruses use both types of PR exonucleases [18]. Furthermore, the DEDD superfamily is further classified into two subfamilies, viz. DEDD(Y) and DEDD(H), depending on whether they employ an invariant Y or a H as the proton acceptor during catalysis [Table 1]. Most of the RNA and DNA viruses possess a typical DEDD superfamily of 3′→5′ PR exoribonuclease in their genome and are well-characterized. For example, in SARS-CoVs and MERS-CoV, it is characterized in the ExoN of the non-structural protein 14 along with the methyltransferase domain [17]. But in the other bat-borne viruses such as Marburg, Ebola and Nipah, a DEDD superfamily of PR exonuclease domain was identified in the PRNTase (the capping enzyme) domain [19]. The DEDD superfamily of PR exonuclease has also been reported in DNA viruses like smallpox, monkeypox viruses, etc. [Table 1] suggesting the same PR mechanism is used by both types of viruses. In contrast to their ubiquitous presence in RNA and DNA viruses, in hantaviruses it was reported that there was no demonstrated, dedicated proofreading exonuclease [20, 21]. However, in the present communication, a putative DEDD superfamily of PR exonuclease domain, preceding the RdRp domain, has been identified featuring an invariant Y as the proton acceptor. 1.3 Importance of 3ʹ→5ʹ PR exonuclease as a potential drug target for controlling RNA viruses Maintenance of genome stability is essential for all living organisms and it mainly relies on the error-free replication of genomes by the respective DNA and RNA replicases. The genome stability is equally important for viruses also. This is because too many uncorrected mutations during replications could lead to an "error catastrophe," where the viruses could literally mutate itself to death. To overcome this problem, the RNA and DNA polymerases/replicases exhibit strong discrimination between nucleoside triphosphates (NTPs) and deoxynucleoside triphosphates (dNTPs) and rarely insert a wrong nucleotide during replication of genomes and hence, their error rates are very, very low and is usually in the order of ~10-4 to 10-6 and ~10-6-10-9, respectively [22]. To overcome even this minimal error rates during replications, these crucial polymerases of life are invariably associated with PR mechanisms that correct any insertion error(s) during replication. When an incorrect nucleotide gets incorporated during replication, the polymerases stall/pause, which in-turn activates the associated PR function, which promptly excises the misincorporated nucleotide. The DEDD superfamily of PR exonucleases operates in the 3’→5’ direction and excise any incorrectly incorporated nucleotide from the 3’-growing end, and thus, helping the polymerases to perform error-free replication of genomes. Following the excision of the wrong nucleotide, the correct nucleotide is inserted and the polymerases resume the replication. This critical PR step in living organisms and viruses ensures that the original DNA/RNA template is copied accurately and passed on to the next generation. For example, with the PR 3'→ 5' exonuclease activity, the error rate dramatically improves to an accuracy of about 10−7 to 10−8 (one mistake per 10 million to 100 million bases). And further, with cellular mismatch repair, the final error rate drops as low as 10−9 to 10−11 per base pair (i.e., about one mistake per 1 billion bases) [23]. Thus, the PR functions play a crucial role in maintaining the integrity of genomes in all organisms including the viruses. It is interesting to note that a SARS-CoV-2 PR exonuclease knockout mutant was unable to replicate, suggesting possibilities for development of effective antivirals directing the PR exonucleases to contain the spread of RNA viruses [17]. 1.4 Genome and L protein organizations in hantaviruses Arenaviridae, Bunyaviridae, and Orthomyxoviridae are the principal families of segmented, negative-strand RNA viruses, and each of them include serious human pathogens. Arenaviridae have two genome segments, whereas Bunyaviridae and Orthomyxoviridae have three and six to eight genome segments, respectively. Arenaviruses and bunyaviruses replicate in the cytoplasm using a single subunit RdRp of the L protein, whereas the orthomyxoviruses replicate in the nucleus- an unusual trait of an RNA virus- using a heterotrimeric polymerase complex composed of PA, PB1 and PB2 subunits [18]. Hantaviruses are segmented, negative-strand, enveloped viruses which belong to the order Bunyavirales, Family, Hantaviridae, and Genus, Orthohantavirus. Unlike other human pathogenic viruses, they are primarily carried by rodents. The virions are generally spherical to pleomorphic, measuring approximately 80-160 nm in diameter, although the size may vary among species. Thus, the segmented, tripartite RNA genome of hantaviruses consists of a small (S), a medium (M), and a large (L) segment and encodes only four structural proteins. The S segment encodes the nucleocapsid (N) protein, which encapsidates viral RNA genome segments to form ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes and plays key roles in viral replication and immune modulation. The M segment encodes a glycoprotein precursor that is post-translationally cleaved into two envelope glycoproteins, Gn and Gc, which are essential for viral attachment and entry into host cells. The multidomain L segment encodes a viral RdRp, responsible for both transcription and replication and a cap- snatching endonuclease, responsible for snatching mRNA caps from the host mRNAs for priming the viral mRNAs. The World Journal of Advanced Research and Reviews, 2026, 32(01), 969–979 972 genomic RNA segments are encapsidated by the nucleocapsid protein P, to form helical RNP complexes, which are enclosed within a host-derived lipid envelope studded with Gn and Gc glycoprotein spikes. [24]. The viral envelope is derived from host cell membranes and contains the above embedded glycoprotein spikes that facilitate interaction with host cell receptors. The tripartite genome segments form into circles via non-covalent interactions of the ends of the genome with an attached L protein to initiate transcription upon entry into host cells. The 3'- and 5'- terminal nucleotides are highly conserved and complementary in all three genome segments that form a conserved panhandle structure acting as the viral promoter in each of the genome segment. In addition to the coding region, each segment possesses short untranslated regions (UTRs) at the 5′ and 3′ termini. The 3' and 5' UTRs are highly conserved and regulate replication and transcription of the genomes [25]. papers.title: Development of a rapid RPA-CRISPR/Cas12b assay for dual detection of Hantaan virus and Seoul virus.
papers.abstract: Hantaan virus (HTNV) and Seoul virus (SEOV) are the primary causative agents of hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), presenting a persistent challenge to global public health. Prompt and precise diagnostic tools are essential for clinical investigation and the containment of HFRS outbreaks. Leveraging the programmable precision of CRISPR/Cas12b system, which has significantly advanced the field of molecular diagnostics, we developed a rapid, high-sensitivity assay for the dual detection of HTNV and SEOV. Each virus was detected in a separate, target-specific single-tube reaction. The assay combines recombinase polymerase amplification (RPA) with CRISPR/Cas12b-mediated fluorescence detection and uses virus-specific sgRNAs and RPA primers targeting conserved genomic regions. Using recombinant plasmid standards, both targets were detected at 1 × 101 copies/test in three technical replicates; this is a preliminary analytical detection threshold and does not incorporate extraction losses or matrix-associated inhibition. No cross-reactivity was observed within the evaluated four-organism non-target panel. In a preliminary feasibility assessment, all nine RT-qPCR-positive rodent samples (seven HTNV and two SEOV) were positive by the RPA-CRISPR/Cas12b assay, indicating complete positive agreement in this all-positive sample set. Because no negative samples were included, negative agreement, diagnostic specificity, false-positive rate, and overall clinical diagnostic accuracy could not be assessed. These results support further development of the assay as a potential screening tool; larger studies using well-characterized positive and negative clinical or field specimens are required.

papers.title_zh: 开发一种快速RPA-CRISPR/Cas12b检测方法,用于双重检测汉滩病毒和首尔病毒。

analysis_zh.background: 汉滩病毒和首尔病毒导致肾综合征出血热,构成全球公共卫生挑战。
analysis_zh.methods: 本研究开发了一种快速高灵敏度检测方法,将重组酶聚合酶扩增(RPA)与CRISPR/Cas12b荧光检测相结合,使用针对保守基因组区域的病毒特异性sgRNA和RPA引物,在单管反应中对每种病毒进行检测。
analysis_zh.results: 分析灵敏度达到1×101拷贝/检测,在三次技术重复中;对四种非目标生物的面板无交叉反应;所有9例RT‐qPCR阳性的啮齿动物样本均被检测到,显示完全阳性一致性。
analysis_zh.contribution: 该检测方法显示出作为HTNV和SEOV双重筛查工具的潜力,支持进一步开发。
analysis_zh.limitations: 检测阈值为初步值,未考虑提取损失或基质抑制;由于缺乏阴性样本,未能评估阴性一致性、特异性、假阳性率及整体准确性;需要使用经充分表征的样本进行更大规模研究。

papers.title: Computational Evaluation of a Novel Nitrothiophene-Derived Schiff Base Ligand Against Breast Cancer-Associated Proteins and Andes Hantavirus Nucleoprotein: Molecular Docking and ADMET Analysis
papers.abstract: The identification of small molecules capable of interacting with multiple therapeutically relevant protein targets is an important strategy in early-stage drug discovery. In the present study, the Schiff base ligand ((N1E,N8E)-N1,N8-bis((5-nitrothiophen-2-yl)methylene)naphthalene-1,8-diamine; N1) was computationally evaluated against a panel of representative disease-associated proteins to investigate its target-binding profile. The primary focus was the assessment of N1 against breast cancer-associated receptor kinases, including EGFR, HER2, VEGFR2, and PI3K, which play central roles in oncogenic signaling pathways. In addition, the Andes hantavirus nucleoprotein was included as an exploratory antiviral target to examine the broader target recognition capability of the ligand rather than to propose a common therapeutic mechanism. Molecular docking studies were performed using AutoDock Vina with experimentally determined protein structures obtained from the Protein Data Bank. N1 demonstrated favorable binding affinities toward all investigated breast cancer targets, with docking scores of −8.708 kcal/mol for EGFR, −8.836 kcal/mol for HER2, −8.906 kcal/mol for VEGFR2, and −9.066 kcal/mol for PI3K. The ligand also exhibited a docking score of −8.8 kcal/mol against the Andes hantavirus nucleoprotein. Interaction analysis revealed multiple stabilizing hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic contacts, electrostatic interactions, and π-mediated interactions within the respective binding pockets.Drug-likeness assessment indicated compliance with Lipinski's and Ghose's rules, while ADMET prediction suggested favorable absorption and membrane permeability. Nevertheless, the predicted risks of hepatotoxicity, cardiotoxicity, and mutagenicity indicate that further structural optimization and experimental validation are required. Overall, this study demonstrates the potential of N1 as a promising scaffold for breast cancer-associated kinase inhibition while providing preliminary evidence of its broader protein-binding capability across biologically distinct targets.

Keywords: Breast cancer, Hantavirus, Molecular docking, Drug-likeness, ADMET, Schiff base Cite This Article: Temitayo O. Aiyelabola, Sayantan Pradhan, and Takashiro Akitsu, “Computational Evaluation of a Novel Nitrothiophene-Derived Schiff Base Ligand Against Breast Cancer-Associated Proteins and Andes Hantavirus Nucleoprotein: Molecular Docking and ADMET Analysis.” Journal of Polymer and Biopolymer Physics Chemistry, vol. 14, no. 1 (2026): 1-14. doi: 10.12691/jpbpc-14-1-1. 1. Introduction Cancer and viral infections remain among the most serious global health challenges due to their high mortality rates, rapid disease progression, and limited availability of effective therapeutic agents [1,2]. Among different malignancies, breast cancer is one of the most frequently diagnosed cancers and represents a leading cause of cancer-related death among women worldwide [3]. The development and progression of breast cancer are closely associated with abnormal activation of receptor tyrosine kinases and intracellular signaling proteins, particularly Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor (EGFR), Human Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor 2 (HER2), Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor Receptor 2 (VEGFR2), and phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) [4,5,6]. These signaling proteins regulate essential cellular processes such as proliferation, angiogenesis, migration, metastasis, survival, and apoptosis. Overexpression or mutation of these targets has been strongly linked with aggressive tumor 2 Journal of Polymer and Biopolymer Physics Chemistry progression and poor clinical prognosis [7]. EGFR and HER2 activation initiates downstream signaling cascades, including the RAS/RAF/MEK/ERK and PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathways, which contribute to uncontrolled cancer cell proliferation, enhanced survival, and metastatic progression (Figure 1) [8,9]. VEGFR2 plays a crucial role in tumor angiogenesis by stimulating endothelial cell migration and vascular formation necessary for tumor growth and metastasis [10]. PI3K, a central component of the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway, regulates cellular growth, proliferation, metabolism, and survival and is frequently dysregulated in breast cancer [11]. Collectively, EGFR, HER2, VEGFR2, and PI3K represent interconnected signaling proteins that regulate complementary aspects of breast cancer progression, including cell proliferation, survival, angiogenesis, and metastasis. Since these proteins belong to functionally linked oncogenic signaling networks, their simultaneous computational evaluation provides an opportunity to investigate whether a single chemical scaffold can potentially interact with multiple biologically relevant targets involved in breast cancer. It should be noted that the present study aims to explore the binding characteristics of N1 toward these proteins through molecular docking and does not imply experimentally validated inhibition of these signaling pathways. Therefore, EGFR, HER2, VEGFR2, and PI3K were selected as representative breast cancer-associated targets for an exploratory computational target-profiling study (Figure 1) [8,9,10,11]. In addition to cancer, viral infections caused by emerging and re-emerging viruses continue to pose major public health concerns worldwide. Andes hantavirus, a member of the Hantaviridae family, is responsible for hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), a severe respiratory disease associated with high fatality rates [12]. The viral nucleoprotein (N protein) plays an essential role in viral RNA encapsidation, ribonucleoprotein complex formation, genome replication, and viral assembly, making it a biologically relevant target for antiviral drug discovery (Figure 2) [13]. Unlike viral enzymes, the nucleoprotein does not possess catalytic activity; instead, its RNA-binding region is responsible for recognizing and stabilizing viral genomic RNA during ribonucleoprotein assembly. Accordingly, the molecular docking analysis in the present study focused on this functionally important RNA-binding region to evaluate the potential molecular recognition of N1. Binding at this site may theoretically interfere with RNA recognition or ribonucleoprotein assembly; however, such effects remain computational hypotheses that require experimental validation [13,14]. The inclusion of the Andes hantavirus nucleoprotein was intended as an exploratory assessment of the binding versatility of the N1 scaffold against a structurally unrelated viral target rather than to propose a unified therapeutic strategy linking breast cancer and hantavirus infection. Despite the severe pathogenicity associated with hantavirus infections, currently available antiviral therapies remain limited, emphasizing the continuing need to identify new antiviral scaffolds for future investigation [14]. In the present work, we report the synthesis and computational evaluation of a novel nitrothiophene- derived Schiff base ligand (N1). The primary objective of this study was to investigate its interaction with multiple breast cancer-associated kinase targets, including EGFR, HER2, VEGFR2, and PI3K, which collectively regulate tumor proliferation, survival, and angiogenesis. As an exploratory extension of this computational investigation, the ligand was also docked against the Andes hantavirus nucleoprotein to assess whether this chemical scaffold exhibits potential binding capability toward a structurally unrelated viral protein involved in RNA encapsidation. This exploratory comparison should not be interpreted as evidence of a unified therapeutic strategy but rather as an initial computational assessment of the molecular recognition properties of N1 across biologically distinct protein targets. The ligand (N1E,N8E)-N1,N8-bis((5- nitrothiophen-2-yl)methylene)naphthalene-1,8-diamine, and its in silico activities are reported here for the first time. Figure 1. The figure illustrates the proposed mechanism of action of the investigated ligand against major breast cancer-associated signaling proteins, including EGFR, HER2, VEGFR2, and PI3K. Activation of EGFR and HER2 normally initiates downstream signaling cascades such as the RAS/RAF/MEK/ERK and PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathways, which promote cancer cell proliferation, survival, and metastasis. VEGFR2 activation stimulates angiogenic signaling pathways responsible for tumor vascularization and endothelial cell migration. In the proposed mechanism, inhibition of these receptors suppresses phosphorylation-mediated signaling events, thereby reducing tumor growth, angiogenesis, and metastatic progression. PI3K inhibition further decreases AKT/mTOR signaling, leading to apoptosis induction and suppression of cancer cell survival. Overall, the figure demonstrates the multi-target inhibitory action of the ligand against critical pathways involved in breast cancer progression Journal of Polymer and Biopolymer Physics Chemistry 3 Figure 2. The figure represents the life cycle of Andes hantavirus and the proposed antiviral mechanism of the investigated compound targeting the viral nucleoprotein (N protein). The hantavirus initially enters the host cell through receptor-mediated endocytosis, followed by viral uncoating and release of ribonucleoprotein complexes into the cytoplasm. Viral RNA transcription and replication are subsequently carried out by the viral RNA- dependent RNA polymerase, leading to synthesis of viral proteins and assembly of new virions. The proposed ligand is suggested to bind within the RNA-binding region of the hantavirus nucleoprotein, thereby interfering with viral RNA encapsidation and ribonucleoprotein complex formation. This inhibition may suppress viral replication, reduce formation of mature viral particles, and prevent further viral dissemination within host cells. The overall antiviral outcome includes inhibition of viral replication, reduction of viral load, and prevention of hantavirus propagation 2. Materials and Methods 2.1. Synthesis: Material All starting materials and solvents used were purchased from Aldrich and Fluka and were used without further purification. Melting points were determined in an open capillary tube on a Gallenkamp (Variable heater) melting point apparatus. NMR spectrum (1H) was recorded on an analysis X-685 benchtop NMR spectrophotometer at 60 MHz DMSO-d6 with TMS as internal standard, at the central science laboratory, Covenant University, Ota. The infrared spectra of all synthesized products were obtained using Agilent Cary 630 FTIR. The electronic spectra, of all the compounds, were obtained in solution, in the wavelength range 400-1000 nm using 1800 Shimadzu ultra-violet spectrophotometer. Both were carried out at the central science laboratory, Obafemi Awolowo University, Ile-Ife. 2.2. Synthesis; Experimental An ethanolic solution of 1,8-diaminonaphthalene (0.83 g, 5.00 mmol) was introduced to a solution of 5-nitro-2- carboxaldehyde (1.62 g, 10.0 mmol) in absolute ethanol (25 mL) supplemented with glacial acetic acid (3 drops) as a catalyst. The reaction mixture was subjected to reflux conditions for 4 hours under atmospheric pressure. Following thermal treatment, the reaction vessel was allowed to equilibrate to ambient temperature, after which the volatile organic solvent was removed via rotary evaporation under reduced pressure until precipitation of a solid product occurred. The crude material was subsequently triturated with cold ethanol and subjected to recrystallization from a chloroform/ethanol solvent mixture (volume ratio 30:70). A deep orange-colored solid was obtained, collected by vacuum filtration, and dried under reduced pressure at 60°C until constant mass was achieved, yielding N1 as the isolated product. The compound demonstrated appreciable solubility in chloroform, ethanol, and methanol. The schematic representation for the preparation of N1 is given in Scheme 1. Yield: 1.49 g, 68.78%; m.p: 165 ̊C - 166 ̊C (d); IR (cm−1): 1608 ν(C=C), 1587 ν(C=N), 1423 ν(C=C, thiophene aromatic ring) 1490 and 1326 ν(NO2), UV-Vis (nm): 299; 1 H NMR (60 MHz): DMSO-d6 δ 7.95 (s, 1H), 7.21, 7.04 (d, 6H), 6.64, 6.55 (d, 2H). Scheme 1. Schematic representation of the synthesis pathway of the novel Schiff base ligand N1, (N1E,N8E)-N1,N8-bis((5-nitrothiophen-2- yl)methylene)naphthalene-1,8-diamine formed through the condensation reaction between 5-nitrothiophene-2-carbaldehyde and naphthalene-1,8- diamine. The figure also illustrates the optimized three-dimensional molecular structure of the synthesized compound 2.3. Retrieval of Protein Structures The three-dimensional crystal structures of the selected 4 Journal of Polymer and Biopolymer Physics Chemistry therapeutic targets associated with breast cancer and viral infection were retrieved from the Protein Data Bank (PDB). The protein structures used in this study included epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR, PDB ID: 1M17, human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2, PDB ID: 3PP0), vascular endothelial growth factor receptor 2 (VEGFR2, PDB ID: 1YWN), phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K, PDB ID: 4JPS), and Andes hantavirus nucleoprotein (PDB ID: 5E04 ). The biologically relevant protein chain (Chain A) was selected for all docking studies. These structures were chosen based on their high crystallographic resolution and the presence of co- crystallized ligands within the active site, allowing accurate definition of the ligand-binding pocket for molecular docking. 2.4. Protein Preparation Protein preparation was performed using AutoDock Tools. Prior to docking, all crystallographic water molecules, co-crystallized ligands, and non-essential heteroatoms were removed while preserving the protein backbone and active-site residues. Polar hydrogen atoms were subsequently added, and Kollman united-atom partial charges were assigned to the protein structures. The prepared receptors were saved in PDBQT format for docking calculations [19]. 2.5. Ligand Preparation The chemical structure of the synthesized ligand was generated using ChemDraw Professional 12.0 and converted into a three-dimensional structure using Avogadro . Geometry optimization was carried out using the MMFF94 force field until convergence to obtain a minimum-energy conformation. Hydrogen atoms were added, appropriate protonation corresponding to physiological pH (approximately 7.4) was assigned, and Gasteiger partial atomic charges were calculated using AutoDock Tools. The optimized ligand was finally converted into PDBQT format for molecular docking [20,21]. 2.6. Molecular Docking Molecular docking studies were performed using AutoDock Vina (version 1.2.7) to evaluate the binding affinity and binding mode of the ligand against the selected protein targets. The docking grid was centered on the active-site region defined by the co-crystallized ligand in each receptor structure. A grid box of 25 × 25 × 25 Å with a grid spacing of 1.0 Å was employed to adequately encompass the entire binding pocket. Docking calculations were carried out using an exhaustiveness value of 8, and 10 binding poses were generated for each protein-ligand complex. The resulting docking conformations were ranked according to their predicted binding free energies (kcal/mol). The optimal binding pose for each complex was selected based on the lowest binding free energy together with a favorable binding orientation and the formation of key interactions with biologically relevant active-site residues identified from the corresponding crystal structures and supported by previous literature [22,23]. 2.7. Drug-Likeness Evaluation The drug-likeness properties of N1 were evaluated using widely accepted computational pharmacokinetic filters, including Lipinski’s Rule of Five and Ghose’s filter, to assess its suitability as a potential orally active therapeutic agent. Physicochemical parameters such as molecular weight, hydrogen bond acceptors, hydrogen bond donors, partition coefficient (logP), molar refractivity, and total number of atoms were calculated to determine the drug-like behavior and oral bioavailability of the compound [24,25]. Lipinski’s Rule of Five was applied based on the criteria of molecular weight below 500 Da, hydrogen bond acceptors fewer than 10, hydrogen bond donors fewer than 5, and logP value below 5, which are considered favorable for oral drug candidates [24]. In addition, Ghose’s filter was employed to further evaluate the compound by considering acceptable ranges of molecular weight, lipophilicity, molar refractivity, and atom count commonly associated with biologically active molecules [25]. All calculations and predictions were performed using an online ADMET and drug-likeness prediction platform. The obtained parameters were analyzed to determine the compliance of N1 with established drug- likeness criteria 2.8. full_text_sections.full_text: Journal of Polymer and Biopolymer Physics Chemistry, 2026, Vol. 14, No. 1, 1-14 Available online at http://pubs.sciepub.com/jpbpc/14/1/1 Published by Science and Education Publishing DOI:10.12691/jpbpc-14-1-1 Computational Evaluation of a Novel Nitrothiophene- Derived Schiff Base Ligand Against Breast Cancer-Associated Proteins and Andes Hantavirus Nucleoprotein: Molecular Docking and ADMET Analysis Temitayo O. Aiyelabola1,*, Sayantan Pradhan2,*, Takashiro Akitsu3 1Department of Chemistry, Faculty of Science, Obafemi Awolowo University, Ile-Ife, Osun State, Nigeria 2Chemical Science Division, Saha Institute of Nuclear Physics, Kolkata, West Bengal, India 3Department of Chemistry, Faculty of Science, Tokyo University of Science, 1-3 Kagurazaka, Shinjuku-ku, Tokyo 162-8601, Japan *Corresponding author: Received August 10, 2026; Revised September 19, 2026; Accepted September 25, 2026 Abstract The identification of small molecules capable of interacting with multiple therapeutically relevant protein targets is an important strategy in early-stage drug discovery. In the present study, the Schiff base ligand ((N1E,N8E)-N1,N8-bis((5-nitrothiophen-2-yl)methylene)naphthalene-1,8-diamine; N1) was computationally evaluated against a panel of representative disease-associated proteins to investigate its target-binding profile. The primary focus was the assessment of N1 against breast cancer-associated receptor kinases, including EGFR, HER2, VEGFR2, and PI3K, which play central roles in oncogenic signaling pathways. In addition, the Andes hantavirus nucleoprotein was included as an exploratory antiviral target to examine the broader target recognition capability of the ligand rather than to propose a common therapeutic mechanism. Molecular docking studies were performed using AutoDock Vina with experimentally determined protein structures obtained from the Protein Data Bank. N1 demonstrated favorable binding affinities toward all investigated breast cancer targets, with docking scores of −8.708 kcal/mol for EGFR, −8.836 kcal/mol for HER2, −8.906 kcal/mol for VEGFR2, and −9.066 kcal/mol for PI3K. The ligand also exhibited a docking score of −8.8 kcal/mol against the Andes hantavirus nucleoprotein. Interaction analysis revealed multiple stabilizing hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic contacts, electrostatic interactions, and π-mediated interactions within the respective binding pockets.Drug-likeness assessment indicated compliance with Lipinski's and Ghose's rules, while ADMET prediction suggested favorable absorption and membrane permeability. Nevertheless, the predicted risks of hepatotoxicity, cardiotoxicity, and mutagenicity indicate that further structural optimization and experimental validation are required. Overall, this study demonstrates the potential of N1 as a promising scaffold for breast cancer-associated kinase inhibition while providing preliminary evidence of its broader protein-binding capability across biologically distinct targets. Keywords: Breast cancer, Hantavirus, Molecular docking, Drug-likeness, ADMET, Schiff base Cite This Article: Temitayo O. Aiyelabola, Sayantan Pradhan, and Takashiro Akitsu, “Computational Evaluation of a Novel Nitrothiophene-Derived Schiff Base Ligand Against Breast Cancer-Associated Proteins and Andes Hantavirus Nucleoprotein: Molecular Docking and ADMET Analysis.” Journal of Polymer and Biopolymer Physics Chemistry, vol. 14, no. 1 (2026): 1-14. doi: 10.12691/jpbpc-14-1-1. 1. Introduction Cancer and viral infections remain among the most serious global health challenges due to their high mortality rates, rapid disease progression, and limited availability of effective therapeutic agents [1,2]. Among different malignancies, breast cancer is one of the most frequently diagnosed cancers and represents a leading cause of cancer-related death among women worldwide [3]. The development and progression of breast cancer are closely associated with abnormal activation of receptor tyrosine kinases and intracellular signaling proteins, particularly Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor (EGFR), Human Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor 2 (HER2), Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor Receptor 2 (VEGFR2), and phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) [4,5,6]. These signaling proteins regulate essential cellular processes such as proliferation, angiogenesis, migration, metastasis, survival, and apoptosis. Overexpression or mutation of these targets has been strongly linked with aggressive tumor 2 Journal of Polymer and Biopolymer Physics Chemistry progression and poor clinical prognosis [7]. EGFR and HER2 activation initiates downstream signaling cascades, including the RAS/RAF/MEK/ERK and PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathways, which contribute to uncontrolled cancer cell proliferation, enhanced survival, and metastatic progression (Figure 1) [8,9]. VEGFR2 plays a crucial role in tumor angiogenesis by stimulating endothelial cell migration and vascular formation necessary for tumor growth and metastasis [10]. PI3K, a central component of the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway, regulates cellular growth, proliferation, metabolism, and survival and is frequently dysregulated in breast cancer [11]. Collectively, EGFR, HER2, VEGFR2, and PI3K represent interconnected signaling proteins that regulate complementary aspects of breast cancer progression, including cell proliferation, survival, angiogenesis, and metastasis. Since these proteins belong to functionally linked oncogenic signaling networks, their simultaneous computational evaluation provides an opportunity to investigate whether a single chemical scaffold can potentially interact with multiple biologically relevant targets involved in breast cancer. It should be noted that the present study aims to explore the binding characteristics of N1 toward these proteins through molecular docking and does not imply experimentally validated inhibition of these signaling pathways. Therefore, EGFR, HER2, VEGFR2, and PI3K were selected as representative breast cancer-associated targets for an exploratory computational target-profiling study (Figure 1) [8,9,10,11]. In addition to cancer, viral infections caused by emerging and re-emerging viruses continue to pose major public health concerns worldwide. Andes hantavirus, a member of the Hantaviridae family, is responsible for hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), a severe respiratory disease associated with high fatality rates [12]. The viral nucleoprotein (N protein) plays an essential role in viral RNA encapsidation, ribonucleoprotein complex formation, genome replication, and viral assembly, making it a biologically relevant target for antiviral drug discovery (Figure 2) [13]. Unlike viral enzymes, the nucleoprotein does not possess catalytic activity; instead, its RNA-binding region is responsible for recognizing and stabilizing viral genomic RNA during ribonucleoprotein assembly. Accordingly, the molecular docking analysis in the present study focused on this functionally important RNA-binding region to evaluate the potential molecular recognition of N1. Binding at this site may theoretically interfere with RNA recognition or ribonucleoprotein assembly; however, such effects remain computational hypotheses that require experimental validation [13,14]. The inclusion of the Andes hantavirus nucleoprotein was intended as an exploratory assessment of the binding versatility of the N1 scaffold against a structurally unrelated viral target rather than to propose a unified therapeutic strategy linking breast cancer and hantavirus infection. Despite the severe pathogenicity associated with hantavirus infections, currently available antiviral therapies remain limited, emphasizing the continuing need to identify new antiviral scaffolds for future investigation [14]. In the present work, we report the synthesis and computational evaluation of a novel nitrothiophene- derived Schiff base ligand (N1). analysis_zh.background: 本研究针对寻找能够结合多个治疗相关蛋白靶点的小分子需求,提出一种在早期药物发现中重要的策略。(A1)
analysis_zh.methods: 作者使用 AutoDock Vina 对硝基噻吩衍生的席夫碱配体 N1 进行计算对接,靶向来自蛋白质数据库的乳腺癌激酶(EGFR、HER2、VEGFR2、PI3K)以及安第斯病毒 汉坦病毒 核蛋白的实验确定结构进行评估。(A2, A6)

analysis_zh.contribution: 作者认为 N1 是抑制乳腺癌相关激酶的有前景骨架,并展示了更广泛的蛋白结合能力,为进一步的抗病毒和抗癌药物研发提供了基础。(A11)
analysis_zh.limitations: 该研究结果仅基于体外计算对接和 ADMET 预测,作者指出预测的毒性以及需要进行结构优化和实验验证。(A10)

papers.title: From Systemic Inflammation to Calcium Leak: The RyR2 Hypothesis of Reversible Myocardial Dysfunction in Andes Virus Cardiopulmonary Syndrome
papers.abstract: Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) caused by Andes virus is a severe zoonotic disease characterized by a paradoxical cardiac phenotype: profound myocardial dysfunction that is frequently reversible in survivors and occurs without extensive structural damage. The mechanisms linking systemic inflammation to this reversible dysfunction remain unknown. This review examines the hypothesis that inflammatory signaling converges on the cardiac ryanodine receptor (RyR2), a major intracellular Ca2+-release channel, through post-translational modifications, generating reversible myocardial dysfunction in HCPS. In severe disease, elevated IL-6, reactive oxygen and nitrogen species, and nitrosative stress activate pathways that in experimental models converge on RyR2 through CaMKII-dependent phosphorylation at Ser2814, oxidative modification of cysteine residues, and S-nitrosylation, each destabilizing the channel and promoting diastolic Ca2+ leak. The resulting increase in spontaneous Ca2+ release reduces SR Ca2+ content, impairs contractility, and predisposes to arrhythmias. This framework identifies RyR2 as a plausible mechanistic hub for the reversible cardiac phenotype. Therapeutic implications are discussed, emphasizing the timing of interventions and the potential of rycals, drugs that stabilize the closed state of RyR2 and prevent diastolic Ca2+ leak, as an emerging strategy. This model provides a testable hypothesis for a disease that currently lacks specific treatment.
