source_records.abstract: Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) caused by Andes virus is a severe zoonotic disease characterized by a paradoxical cardiac phenotype: profound myocardial dysfunction that is frequently reversible in survivors and occurs without extensive structural damage. This model provides a testable hypothesis for a disease that currently lacks specific treatment.

analysis.background: Andes virus causes hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) with profound but reversible myocardial dysfunction and little structural damage (A1).
analysis.main_directions: The review proposes that systemic inflammation activates CaMKII, oxidative, and nitrosylation pathways that modify RyR2, causing diastolic Ca²⁺ leak and contractile impairment (A3,A4,A5,A6).
analysis.current_state: Current knowledge recognizes HCPS’s reversible cardiac phenotype and the potential central role of RyR2, but definitive mechanistic links remain unproven (A1,A3,A4).
analysis.gaps: Key uncertainties include the precise inflammatory triggers, the extent of RyR2 modification, arrhythmia risk, and lack of specific therapies (A2,A5,A7,A8).
analysis.future_research: Future work should experimentally validate RyR2 modifications, assess rycal efficacy and timing, and develop targeted interventions (A7,A8).

analysis.summary_en: Background: Andes virus HCPS presents reversible myocardial dysfunction with minimal structural damage (A1). Main directions: Inflammation may modify RyR2 via CaMKII, oxidation, and nitrosylation, leading to Ca²⁺ leak and contractile failure (A3,A4,A5,A6). Current state: The reversible cardiac phenotype is documented, but mechanistic evidence is incomplete (A1,A3,A4). Gaps: Unclear inflammatory triggers, RyR2 modification extent, arrhythmia risk, and no specific treatments (A2,A5,A7,A8). Future research: Validate RyR2 changes experimentally, test rycal timing and efficacy, and pursue targeted therapies (A7,A8).

papers.title: Hantaviral therapeutics: life cycle targets and chemotherapeutic interventions
papers.abstract: Orthohantaviruses represent a persistent global health threat, being responsible for life-threatening diseases such as Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome (HFRS) and Hantavirus Cardiopulmonary Syndrome (HCPS). Despite high case fatality rates and recent outbreaks, there are currently no universally licensed antivirals or vaccines. Clinical management remains heavily reliant on supportive care and repurposed drugs, which often exhibit limited efficacy and dose-limiting toxicities. This review examines rational drug design strategies targeting critical steps in the viral life cycle, specifically Gn/Gc-mediated cellular entry and RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp)-driven genome replication. We evaluate the current landscape of viral inhibitors, including peptidomimetics, nucleoside analogues, and naturally derived compounds. To accelerate the discovery of novel treatments, we advocate for the integration of modern in silico screening to evaluate extensive chemical and natural product libraries. These broad compound collections offer a structurally diverse and largely untapped reservoir for antiviral development. Ultimately, expanding preclinical testing to include globally neglected variants will be essential to develop broad-spectrum hantaviral therapeutics capable of mitigating future epidemic threats.

KEYWORDS antiviral discovery, drug development, orthohantavirus, chemotherapeutics, phytochemicals, viral entry inhibitors, RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) inhibitors, viral life cycle targets Introduction The April 2026 Andes hantavirus outbreak on a cruise ship served as a reminder of the ongoing challenges pathogens pose to global public health (Andes Virus Outbreak Working Group, 2026; Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2026; World Health Organization, 2026b). The high case fatality rate highlights that there are currently no universally licensed antivirals or vaccines against orthohantavirus infections (World Health Organization, 2026a). These rodent-borne pathogens belong to the family Hantaviridae, genus Orthohantavirus, and are enveloped, tri-segmented, single-stranded negative-sense RNA viruses (Jonsson et al., 2010). They cause two distinct, life-threatening clinical syndromes, one being Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome (HFRS) in Eurasia, and Hantavirus Cardiopulmonary Syndrome (HCPS) in the Americas (Heyman et al., 2009). Once internalized via endocytosis, a drop in endosomal pH forces the viral envelope to fuse with the host membrane, releasing the genome into the cytoplasm. The viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) starts both transcription and genome replication, before structural proteins and newly synthesized RNA assemble at the Golgi complex or plasma membrane prior to budding out as mature infectious virions (see Figure 1) (Hussein et al., 2011; Hepojoki et al., 2012; Vaheri et al., 2013b; Bradfute et al., 2024). This peptide was further refined to its minimal functional unit required through alanine substitution and deletion scanning to the cyclic pentapeptide cyclo-[CPFVC] (Hall et al., 2007). However, because free monovalent peptides were less effec- tive than those presented on phage, subsequent research (Hall et al., 2008) shifted towards presenting peptides in a multivalent format on nanoparticles and targeting the orthohantavirus glycoproteins directly rather than the host b3-integrin receptor. The three most potent binders of the virion were selected and attached to 100 nm nanoparticles to create a multivalent inhibitor. When the peptide CLVRNLAWC was presented on a nanoparticle at a 4:1 ratio, its inhibition of SNV jumped from 9% (as a free peptide) to 32.5%. However, the peptide CQATTARNC achieved an even higher efficacy, with inhibition surpassing 50% when the nanoparticle- to-virus ratio was increased to 20:1 (Hall et al., 2008). Building on these strategies, the research was expanded to Andes virus (ANDV). Using a similar approach, Hall et al. (2009) eluted the peptide library from purified ANDV particles using monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) against the Gn and Gc glycoproteins. A major finding in this study was the combined use of peptides that targeted different Gn- and Gc-specific sequences resulted in synergistic inhibition (anti-Gc/Gn peptides CMQSAAAHC and CTVGPTRSC) of infec- tion that was significantly more powerful than single-peptide treatments, emphasizing the benefit of targeting multiple viral epitopes (Hall et al., 2009). Lastly, to search for peptidomimetic molecules to block SNV infection, Hall et al. (2010) used the 3D structure of the previously refined pentapeptide cyclo-[CPFVC], in a ligand-based virtual screening approach to evaluate over 600,000 small molecules. This transition from biological peptides to drug- like peptidomimetics identified compounds such as G319–0078 and 8012-0652, which were 2,000 times more potent than the original cyclic peptides. These molecules demonstrated high-affinity inhibi- tion in the nanomolar range in vitro (EC50 values between 1.3 - 2.5 nM) (Hall et al., 2010), successfully evolving the initial lead into a highly potent preclinical candidate warranting further in vivo evaluation. Another distinct strategy to prevent infection focuses on dis- rupting the viral membrane fusion process. Because the orthohantavirus Gc glycoprotein functions as a class II fusion protein, completing membrane fusion requires a major structural relocation of Domain III (DIII) to achieve the post-fusion state (Barriga et al., 2016; Arata-Salas et al., 2026). Exploiting this mechanical vulnerability, Barriga et al. (2016) demonstrated that viral entry can be successfully blocked using recombinant fragments and synthetic peptides derived from the Gc DIII and stem region. These fragments allow initial Gc trimerization to proceed but ultimately inhibit the pathway by preventing membrane hemifusion and fusion pore formation (Barriga et al., 2016). The recombinant DIII fragment inhibited ANDV fusion by around 70% at 25 μM and demonstrated cross-reactivity by reducing PUUV-mediated fusion by 50%. Even greater potency was observed with the R2 peptide, derived from the C-terminal part of the Gc stem region, which inhibited ANDV fusion by up to 95% in vitro (Barriga et al., 2016). Although efficacy dropped to a 70% cross-reduction (at 20 μM) against PUUV-mediated fusion (Barriga et al., 2016) due to its high genetic divergence between the two viruses, it still demonstrates significant cross-protective potential. Another very potent cell-entry inhibitor is Griffithsin (GRFT), an algae-derived lectin that has demonstrated high efficacy against several enveloped viruses such as coronaviruses, retroviruses, lentiviruses, flaviviruses, hepaciviruses, paramyxoviruses, and her- pesviruses, with the notable exclusion of gamma- and delta-retro- viruses. Interestingly, GRFT is also effective against the non- enveloped human papillomavirus (HPV), where it acts during a late step in the viral entry process rather than during initial attachment (O’Keefe et al., 2010; Lusvarghi and Bewley, 2016). In vivo administration of GRFT demonstrated clear therapeutic effi- cacy, significantly mitigating disease severity and reducing mortality in lethal SARS-CoV infection models (O’Keefe et al., 2010). Highlighting its strong translational potential, GRFT has also advanced to phase I clinical trials against human immunodeficiency virus (HIV-1) infections (ClinicalTrials.gov Identifiers: NCT04032717, NCT02875119). In addition to potent inhibition of ANDV entry (Shrivastava-Ranjan et al., 2020), found that a synthetic trimeric variant (3mGRFT) possessing nine oligosaccha- ride-binding sites demonstrated even greater in vitro potency against ANDV and SNV. However, in contrast to its post-infection efficacy seen in other viral models (Lusvarghi and Bewley, 2016), the authors observed that GRFT lacked potent inhibitory activity against ANDV post-infection. While GRFT showed in vitro effec- tivity against New World hantaviruses (Shrivastava-Ranjan et al., 2020), the lectin inhibited HTNV in vivo and provided partial protection in suckling mice infected with HTNV (Zhao et al., 2022). Moreover, GRFT can be produced on a large scale and can be easily purified, highlighting its potential as an antiviral candidate for further preclinical testing against orthohantaviruses (Zhao et al., 2022). Exploring natural host defense proteins, bovine lactoferrin (LF) has demonstrated significant efficacy as a viral inhibitor against SEOV. LF prevents initial viral adsorption and adhesion, likely by interacting with cellular glycosaminoglycans such as heparin, or by sterically hindering the virus from binding to host b-integrin and lectin receptors (Murphy et al., 2000, 2001). Importantly, LF has no antiviral effect once the virus entered the host cell. In vivo, prophylactic administration of LF one day prior to orthohantavirus inoculation improved survival rates in mice up to 70% (at 160 mg/ kg), with a double-administration regimen enhancing survival to over 94%. Furthermore, when prophylactic LF treatment was combined with subsequent ribavirin administration, the two agents functioned synergistically, profoundly reducing viral shed- ding and completely inhibiting viral protein expression (Murphy et al., 2000, 2001). Discovered through a high-throughput screening of over 2,300 approved drugs and traditional Chinese medicines, cepharanthine (CEP), which is a compound isolated from Stephania cephalantha Hayata, has emerged as a highly potent viral entry and membrane fusion inhibitor. In vitro, CEP inhibited HTNV pseudovirus (EC50 value of 0.9 μM) and reduced viral nucleic acid copies by 73% at 20 μM. In vivo, administering CEP to Balb/c mice five hours post- infection significantly reduced infection by 93% (at 90 mg/kg/day) and 94% (at 180 mg/kg/day). Given its established safety profile, Kocabiyik et al. 10.3389/fcimb.2026.1972830 Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology frontiersin.org 03 CEP represents a high-priority candidate for repurposing and advancement into human clinical trials against orthohantaviruses (Wen et al., 2022). Viral replication and polymerase inhibitors Ribavirin (1-b- D-ribofuranosyl-1H-1,2,4-triazole-3- carboxamide; RBV), a synthetic guanosine nucleoside analogue, serves as the historical benchmark for anti-hantaviral therapy (Sidwell et al., 1972). Once it is transported into host cells, RBV is rapidly phosphorylated into metabolites such as RBV-5’-mono- phosphate (RBV-MP) and RBV-5’-triphosphate (RBV-TP). While RBV-MP inhibits inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase (IMPDH), resulting in a decrease in intracellular GTP levels, RBV-TP selectively interacts with the viral RdRp as its primary mechanism of action (Severson et al., 2003; Sun et al., 2007). The incorporation of RBV leads to accumulation of genomic errors, and thus to dramatic loss of virus viability (“error catastrophe”) (Severson et al., 2003; Chung et al., 2007). Preclinical evaluation confirmed that early RBV administration reduces viral loads and prevents severe disease in suckling mouse models infected with Hantaan virus (HTNV) and hamster models infected with Andes virus (ANDV) (Huggins et al., 1986; Ogg et al., 2013). Clinically, intravenous RBV demonstrated efficacy in a double-blind, placebo- controlled trial of 242 patients with HTNV-induced HFRS, signif- icantly reducing hemorrhagic and overall mortality (Huggins et al., 1991). Trials in HFRS caused by Puumala virus (PUUV) also showed insufficient efficacy and safety of intravenous RBV, likely due to delayed drug administra- tion and weaker correlation between viral load and disease severity compared to HTNV infection (Malinin and Platonov, 2017). Despite its status as an established treatment for HFRS, the clinical utility of RBV is constrained by dose-limiting toxicities, most notably reversible hemolytic anemia, reported in 71% of recipients (Chapman et al., 1999; Jonsson et al., 2010). Furthermore, the lack of efficacy in HCPS and PUUV-caused HFRS is attributed to the rapid clinical progression of these diseases, which often leaves a narrow window for intervention before the onset of irreversible organ failure (Heyman et al., 2009; Vaheri et al., 2013a; Strella et al., 2025). This active metabolite functions as a purine nucleotide analogue that is incorporated into nascent viral RNA, inducing lethal mutagenesis in the viral genome (Furuta et al., 2009, 2017). Safronetz et al. (2013) have shown that favipiravir potently inhibited ANDV and SNV in vitro, and provided 100% survival in lethal ANDV hamster models when treatment was initiated before viremia, making it an important drug candidate for post-exposure prophylaxis. full_text_sections.full_text: Hantaviral therapeutics: life cycle targets and chemotherapeutic interventions Deren Zehra Kocabiyik 1,2, Jansen de Araujo 3, Edison Luiz Durigon 2,3* and Carsten Wrenger 1,2* 1Unit for Drug Discovery, Department of Parasitology, Institute of Biomedical Sciences, University of São Paulo, São Paulo, Brazil, 2Institut Pasteur de São Paulo, São Paulo, Brazil, 3Department of Microbiology, Institute of Biomedical Sciences, University of São Paulo, São Paulo, Brazil Orthohantaviruses represent a persistent global health threat, being responsible for life-threatening diseases such as Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome (HFRS) and Hantavirus Cardiopulmonary Syndrome (HCPS). Despite high case fatality rates and recent outbreaks, there are currently no universally licensed antivirals or vaccines. Clinical management remains heavily reliant on supportive care and repurposed drugs, which often exhibit limited efficacy and dose-limiting toxicities. This review examines rational drug design strategies targeting critical steps in the viral life cycle, specifically Gn/Gc-mediated cellular entry and RNA- dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp)-driven genome replication. We evaluate the current landscape of viral inhibitors, including peptidomimetics, nucleoside analogues, and naturally derived compounds. To accelerate the discovery of novel treatments, we advocate for the integration of modern in silico screening to evaluate extensive chemical and natural product libraries. These broad com- pound collections offer a structurally diverse and largely untapped reservoir for antiviral development. Ultimately, expanding preclinical testing to include globally neglected variants will be essential to develop broad-spectrum hantaviral ther- apeutics capable of mitigating future epidemic threats. The high case fatality rate highlights that there are currently no universally licensed antivirals or vaccines against orthohantavirus infections (World Health Organization, 2026a). These rodent-borne pathogens belong to the family Hantaviridae, genus Orthohantavirus, and are enveloped, tri-segmented, single-stranded negative-sense RNA viruses (Jonsson et al., 2010). analysis.background: Orthohantaviruses cause life‑threatening HFRS and HCPS and remain a persistent global health threat.
analysis.main_directions: The review emphasizes rational drug design against Gn/Gc‑mediated entry and RdRp‑driven replication, and surveys peptidomimetics, nucleoside analogues and natural compounds.
analysis.current_state: No universally licensed antivirals or vaccines exist; clinical management relies on supportive care and repurposed drugs that show limited efficacy and dose‑limiting toxicity.
analysis.gaps: Effective broad‑spectrum therapeutics are lacking, preclinical testing on diverse and neglected hantavirus variants is insufficient, and many candidate inhibitors remain unevaluated.
analysis.future_research: Adopt modern in‑silico screening of large chemical and natural product libraries, expand preclinical evaluation to under‑studied hantavirus strains, and advance rational design of entry and polymerase inhibitors toward broad‑spectrum antivirals.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Orthohantaviruses cause HFRS and HCPS, representing a persistent global health threat. Main directions: The review focuses on rational drug design targeting Gn/Gc entry and RdRp replication, evaluating peptidomimetics, nucleoside analogues and natural compounds. Current state: No licensed antivirals or vaccines exist; care is supportive with repurposed drugs of limited efficacy. Gaps: Effective broad‑spectrum therapeutics and comprehensive preclinical testing of diverse variants are lacking. Future research: Integrate in‑silico docking of extensive chemical/natural libraries, broaden preclinical testing to neglected strains, and advance entry and polymerase inhibitor design for broad‑spectrum hantaviral antivirals.

papers.title_zh: 汉坦病毒治疗学:生命周期靶点与化学治疗干预

analysis_zh.background: 正汉坦病毒导致危及生命的肾综合征出血热(HFRS)和汉坦病毒心肺综合征(HCPS),并仍然是持续的全球健康威胁。
analysis_zh.main_directions: 本综述强调针对Gn/Gc介导的进入和RdRp驱动的复制的合理药物设计,并概述肽仿制物、核苷类似物和天然化合物。
analysis_zh.current_state: 目前尚无普遍获批的抗病毒药物或疫苗;临床管理依赖支持性治疗和已重新用于治疗的药物,但其疗效有限且存在剂量限制性毒性。
analysis_zh.gaps: 缺乏有效的广谱治疗剂,对多样且被忽视的汉坦病毒变体的临床前测试不足,且许多候选抑制剂仍未评估。
analysis_zh.future_research: 采用现代的计算筛选,对大型化学和天然产物库进行筛选,将临床前评估扩展至研究不足的汉坦病毒株系,并推进针对进入和聚合酶抑制剂的合理设计,以实现广谱抗病毒药物。

papers.title: Hantavirus emergence through a One Health lens: ecological dynamics, human exposure and integrated surveillance
papers.abstract: Abstract Hantaviruses are rodent-borne zoonotic viruses that cause haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome in Eurasia and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome in the Americas. Although human hantavirus infections are usually recognised clinically, infection risk is affected by upstream factors including reservoir-host ecology, environmental variability and human exposure. Evidence from China, Europe and the Americas shows that the incidence of hantavirus may depend on rodent population dynamics, climate conditions, land use, agricultural practices, housing environments and recreational or travel-related exposure. In China, the seasonal pattern of haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, including a major autumn–winter peak and a smaller spring or spring–summer peak in many endemic areas, illustrates how virus–host ecology and agricultural labour jointly affect the human risk. In Europe, bank vole population cycles have been shown to influence Puumala virus epidemics, while studies in the Americas have linked rainfall, rodent abundance and human exposure in domestic, occupational and recreational settings. This mini review synthesises evidence on the ecological drivers, exposure pathways and surveillance challenges for hantavirus diseases through a One Health lens. We suggest that One Health approaches should move beyond general calls for multisector collaboration towards evidence-informed surveillance linking rodent, environmental and human data to setting-specific prevention, such as issuing seasonal risk warnings and reinforcing exposure-reduction measures before harvest periods in endemic agricultural regions.

Hantavirus emergence through a One Health lens: ecological dynamics, human exposure and integrated surveillance Xinyu Wang1,2* Abstract Hantaviruses are rodent-borne zoonotic viruses that cause haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome in Eurasia and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome in the Americas. Although human hantavirus infections are usually recognised clinically, infection risk is affected by upstream factors including reservoir-host ecology, environmental variability and human exposure. Evidence from China, Europe and the Americas shows that the incidence of hantavi- rus may depend on rodent population dynamics, climate conditions, land use, agricultural practices, housing environ- ments and recreational or travel-related exposure. In China, the seasonal pattern of haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, including a major autumn–winter peak and a smaller spring or spring–summer peak in many endemic areas, illustrates how virus–host ecology and agricultural labour jointly affect the human risk. In Europe, bank vole population cycles have been shown to influence Puumala virus epidemics, while studies in the Americas have linked rainfall, rodent abundance and human exposure in domestic, occupational and recreational settings. This mini review synthesises evidence on the ecological drivers, exposure pathways and surveillance challenges for hantavirus diseases through a One Health lens. We suggest that One Health approaches should move beyond general calls for multisec- tor collaboration towards evidence-informed surveillance linking rodent, environmental and human data to setting- specific prevention, such as issuing seasonal risk warnings and reinforcing exposure-reduction measures before har- vest periods in endemic agricultural regions. Keywords Hantavirus, One Health, Haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome, Rodent reservoir, Ecological surveillance, China, Travel medicine Introduction The epidemiology of hantaviruses is tightly linked to res- ervoir hosts, environmental conditions and human expo- sure, making them a useful model for reviewing zoonotic emergence through a One Health lens. Medically impor- tant hantaviruses are maintained primarily in rodent reservoirs and are associated with two major human disease syndromes: haemorrhagic fever with renal syn- drome (HFRS), reported mainly in Europe and Asia, and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS; also his- torically referred to as hantavirus pulmonary syndrome), reported mainly in the Americas [1–3]. Human infec- tion is usually accidental and occurs when people enter environments contaminated by infectious rodent excreta; however, Andes virus remains the major exception, with documented person-to-person transmission under con- ditions of close or prolonged contact [3, 4]. Rather than cataloguing hantavirus species, this review focuses on synthesising the evidence for how ecological *Correspondence: Xinyu Wang snowmed@gmail.com 1 Department of Infectious Diseases, Huashan Hospital, Fudan University, Shanghai 200040, China 2 National Medical Center for Infectious Diseases, Shanghai 200040, China Page 2 of 7 Wang ﻿One Health Advances (2026) 4:36 and social processes shape human infection. Key ques- tions are not only which virus is carried by which rodent, but under what environmental and behavioural condi- tions infected reservoirs and susceptible humans are brought into contact. This framing is relevant for the One Health approach, because hantavirus risk can be exam- ined across measurable links including the rodent popu- lation density, reservoir-infection prevalence, climate variability, land use, agricultural or occupational expo- sure, housing conditions, recreational travel and clinical surveillance [1, 5]. China’s long-standing HFRS experi- ence, Europe’s cyclic Puumala virus epidemics and HCPS outbreaks in the Americas collectively provide comple- mentary evidence for understanding hantavirus emer- gence as an integrated human–animal–environment problem. This makes hantavirus disease a useful case for examining how the One Health approach can move from a conceptual framework to measurable surveillance indi- cators and setting-specific prevention. Reservoir ecology and environmental drivers of hantavirus risk The geographic distribution of hantavirus infection is strongly affected by its reservoir-host ecology. Although an increasing variety of hantaviruses have been detected in mammals, medically important hantaviruses are mainly maintained in rodent reservoirs, and many patho- genic viruses show close associations with particular host species or host complexes [1, 2]. This host dependence helps to explain the geographically uneven hantavirus risk, with human disease only occurring where compe- tent reservoirs, suitable habitats and human exposure all overlap. However, reservoir presence alone is insuf- ficient to predict human risk, and the local incidence also depends on rodent abundance, infection prevalence within reservoir populations, seasonal movement, habi- tat disturbance and the frequency with which humans enter contaminated environments [5]. Environmental variability can influence hantavirus transmission by changing the reservoir-host population dynamics and human–rodent contact. Increased rain- fall may enhance vegetation growth and food availabil- ity for rodents, thus supporting their reproduction and survival, while drought, habitat disruption or cold stress may drive rodents into human dwellings, storage areas or workplaces. The Four Corners region of the southwestern United States remains a classic example, where El Niño- associated precipitation led to ecological conditions that favoured increases in deer mouse populations, with a subsequent marked increase in HCPS cases in affected areas [6]. In Europe, Puumala virus epidemics have been linked to bank vole population cycles influenced by for- est ecology, food availability and seasonal conditions [7]. These examples suggest that climate is not a direct cause in isolation, but can influence risk via reservoir ecology and exposure pathways. Because human hantavirus cases often occur after changes in reservoir populations, rodent abundance and infection prevalence can act as early-warning indicators. Long-term ecological studies in Europe and the Americas have shown that rodent population cycles may precede changes in human disease risk [6, 7]. In China, ecologi- cal studies of HFRS have also emphasised the interacting roles of environmental variability, reservoir ecology and human behaviour in shaping disease dynamics [5]. These findings support a practical One Health implication: rodent monitoring should not be treated solely as ecolog- ical research, but as part of an integrated risk-assessment system linking animal, environmental and human health data. Land use, agriculture and human exposure: evidence from China and beyond Land use determines how often reservoir hosts, con- taminated environments and susceptible humans share the same space. Agricultural expansion, crop harvesting, grain storage, peri-domestic farming structures, forest edges and poorly sealed rural housing can increase the opportunities for contact with rodent excreta. A system- atic review of land cover, land use and human hantavi- rus infection risk found that agricultural land use was positively associated with infection risk in several set- tings, particularly in China and Brazil, whereas associa- tions with forest cover, grassland or built-up areas varied by region and virus ecology [8]. This heterogeneity is important, in that land use is not a universal risk factor but rather modifies exposure through local combinations of reservoir species, farming systems, housing conditions and human behaviour. China provides one of the clearest examples of how virus ecology and human activity jointly structure hanta- virus seasonality. In many endemic areas, HFRS shows a bimodal pattern, with a larger autumn–winter peak and a smaller spring or spring–summer peak. In China, this bimodal pattern has often been interpreted as reflect- ing the coexistence of different virus–host systems and exposure settings. Hantaan virus, mainly associated with Apodemus agrarius, contributes more to field or rural exposure and autumn–winter incidence, whereas Seoul virus, carried by Rattus norvegicus, is more relevant to peri-domestic or urban transmission and spring inci- dence in many settings [9–11]. In Zibo City, HFRS cases peaked during March–May and October–December, illustrating the seasonal human risk pattern [9]. Spatial analyses from the same region further suggested that Page 3 of 7 Wang ﻿One Health Advances (2026) 4:36 spring and autumn risks differed geographically, support- ing targeted seasonal prevention [12]. The link between agricultural activity and HFRS sea- sonality is particularly evident in high-incidence prov- inces such as Shandong. A time-series analysis reported marked seasonality and discussed the temporal cor- respondence between agricultural activity and HFRS incidence: the autumn harvest usually begins in late September, cases then rise rapidly in October, peak in November, and decline in December [13]. The incubation period of hantavirus infection suggests that this pattern is biologically plausible and consistent with exposure dur- ing harvesting, field work, grain handling or temporary accommodation in rodent-infested settings. Together with the smaller spring peak observed in many endemic areas, this pattern suggests that HFRS risk is shaped by seasonally changing combinations of reservoir ecology, agricultural labour and peri-domestic exposure, rather than by a single constant pathway. In addition to agriculture, hantavirus exposure may occur in occupational, domestic, recreational and travel settings. Farmers, forestry workers, construction work- ers, cleaners, military personnel and people entering rodent-infested buildings may experience intense short- term exposure when contaminated dust is disturbed. Recreational exposure can occur when visitors stay in cabins, campsites or enclosed structures with rodent infestation. The 2012 Yosemite National Park outbreak, linked to overnight stays in insulated tent cabins, showed how built environments can convert local rodent ecology into visitor risk [14]. The 2026 cruise-associated Andes virus cluster illustrates a different pathway, with local ecological exposure potentially becoming a multi-coun- try public health problem when combined with delayed recognition, confined travel settings and international movements [15]. Surveillance evidence and gaps across human– animal–environment systems China’s long-term HFRS experience provides an instruc- tive example of surveillance that already contains several One Health elements, even if not always labelled as such. National surveillance has combined human case report- ing with rodent surveillance, laboratory testing and tar- geted prevention in endemic areas. During 2006–2012, 77,558 HFRS cases and 866 deaths were reported in China. Cases were clustered in a small number of prov- inces and occurring mainly in spring and autumn–win- ter seasons, with farmers remaining the largest affected occupational group [10]. More recent national data for 2014–2023 show continuing geographic and virological complexity, with Hantaan virus, Seoul virus and Puu- mala virus among the identified human HFRS-associated hantaviruses in China [11]. These regional contrasts are summarised in Table 1, which compares rodent, envi- ronmental and human surveillance components across China, Europe and the Americas. Despite the value of long-term case reporting, human surveillance alone is inherently too late for hantavirus prevention, and human cases usually only appear after ecological changes, rodent population shifts and expo- sure events have already occurred. Clinical recogni- tion may also be delayed because the early symptoms are non-specific and overlap with leptospirosis, dengue, influenza-like illness, malaria, COVID-19 and other febrile syndromes [3]. This is particularly relevant in rural or travel-related settings, where the exposure event may be remote in time and place from the diagnosis. For surveillance to support prevention rather than only documentation, clinical signals should be connected with rodent, environmental and exposure information. In clinical practice, a compatible syndrome combined with a carefully reconstructed exposure history—such as recent rural residence, crop harvesting, cleaning of rodent-infested spaces, cabin stay or expedition travel— may provide the first actionable signal before laboratory confirmation. The One Health challenge is therefore not simply to collect more data, but to link the appropriate data to timely decisions. Information on rodent density, reser- voir infection prevalence, climate anomalies, agricultural calendars, land-use changes, clinical syndromes and travel or occupational histories is often held by different sectors and interpreted separately. Broader One Health early-warning literature emphasises the importance of bottom-up reporting and grassroots actors for reduc- ing delays between outbreak emergence, notification and response [16]. For hantavirus diseases, integrated early warning should therefore be judged not by the number of assembled datasets, but by whether ecological and clinical signals lead to earlier, setting-specific preven- tion. Future surveillance should therefore be built around predefined risk questions and response thresholds rather than around parallel human, animal and environmental datasets. In resource-limited settings, integrated One Health surveillance should not aim to monitor every possible ecological, animal and human indicator. A more feasible approach is to develop a minimum surveillance package tailored to local risk settings, combining routine report- ing of compatible human syndromes, simple rodent-den- sity indicators, seasonal agricultural calendars, rainfall or flooding alerts, community reports of rodent infestation and exposure histories collected during clinical assess- ment. Standardised metrics could include monthly rodent density, the proportion of captured rodents test- ing positive, rainfall deviation from the seasonal baseline, the number of compatible human cases, the proportion with documented exposure history and the number of high-risk settings receiving seasonal risk communication. In Europe, bank vole population cycles have been shown to influence Puumala virus epidemics, while studies in the Americas have linked rainfall, rodent abundance and human exposure in domestic, occupational and recreational settings. This mini review synthesises evidence on the ecological drivers, exposure pathways and surveillance challenges for hantavirus diseases through a One Health lens. We suggest that One Health approaches should move beyond general calls for multisec- tor collaboration towards evidence-informed surveillance linking rodent, environmental and human data to setting- specific prevention, such as issuing seasonal risk warnings and reinforcing exposure-reduction measures before har- vest periods in endemic agricultural regions. Keywords Hantavirus, One Health, Haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome, Rodent reservoir, Ecological surveillance, China, Travel medicine Introduction The epidemiology of hantaviruses is tightly linked to res- ervoir hosts, environmental conditions and human expo- sure, making them a useful model for reviewing zoonotic emergence through a One Health lens. Medically impor- tant hantaviruses are maintained primarily in rodent reservoirs and are associated with two major human disease syndromes: haemorrhagic fever with renal syn- drome (HFRS), reported mainly in Europe and Asia, and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS; also his- torically referred to as hantavirus pulmonary syndrome), reported mainly in the Americas [1–3]. Human infec- tion is usually accidental and occurs when people enter environments contaminated by infectious rodent excreta; however, Andes virus remains the major exception, with documented person-to-person transmission under con- ditions of close or prolonged contact [3, 4]. Rather than cataloguing hantavirus species, this review focuses on synthesising the evidence for how ecological *Correspondence: Xinyu Wang snowmed@gmail.com 1 Department of Infectious Diseases, Huashan Hospital, Fudan University, Shanghai 200040, China 2 National Medical Center for Infectious Diseases, Shanghai 200040, China Page 2 of 7 Wang ﻿One Health Advances (2026) 4:36 and social processes shape human infection. Key ques- tions are not only which virus is carried by which rodent, but under what environmental and behavioural condi- tions infected reservoirs and susceptible humans are brought into contact. This framing is relevant for the One Health approach, because hantavirus risk can be exam- ined across measurable links including the rodent popu- lation density, reservoir-infection prevalence, climate variability, land use, agricultural or occupational expo- sure, housing conditions, recreational travel and clinical surveillance [1, 5]. China’s long-standing HFRS experi- ence, Europe’s cyclic Puumala virus epidemics and HCPS outbreaks in the Americas collectively provide comple- mentary evidence for understanding hantavirus emer- gence as an integrated human–animal–environment problem. This makes hantavirus disease a useful case for examining how the One Health approach can move from a conceptual framework to measurable surveillance indi- cators and setting-specific prevention. Reservoir ecology and environmental drivers of hantavirus risk The geographic distribution of hantavirus infection is strongly affected by its reservoir-host ecology. Although an increasing variety of hantaviruses have been detected in mammals, medically important hantaviruses are mainly maintained in rodent reservoirs, and many patho- genic viruses show close associations with particular host species or host complexes [1, 2]. This host dependence helps to explain the geographically uneven hantavirus risk, with human disease only occurring where compe- tent reservoirs, suitable habitats and human exposure all overlap. However, reservoir presence alone is insuf- ficient to predict human risk, and the local incidence also depends on rodent abundance, infection prevalence within reservoir populations, seasonal movement, habi- tat disturbance and the frequency with which humans enter contaminated environments [5]. Environmental variability can influence hantavirus transmission by changing the reservoir-host population dynamics and human–rodent contact. Increased rain- fall may enhance vegetation growth and food availabil- ity for rodents, thus supporting their reproduction and survival, while drought, habitat disruption or cold stress may drive rodents into human dwellings, storage areas or workplaces. The Four Corners region of the southwestern United States remains a classic example, where El Niño- associated precipitation led to ecological conditions that favoured increases in deer mouse populations, with a subsequent marked increase in HCPS cases in affected areas [6]. In Europe, Puumala virus epidemics have been linked to bank vole population cycles influenced by for- est ecology, food availability and seasonal conditions [7]. These examples suggest that climate is not a direct cause in isolation, but can influence risk via reservoir ecology and exposure pathways. Because human hantavirus cases often occur after changes in reservoir populations, rodent abundance and infection prevalence can act as early-warning indicators. Long-term ecological studies in Europe and the Americas have shown that rodent population cycles may precede changes in human disease risk [6, 7]. In China, ecologi- cal studies of HFRS have also emphasised the interacting roles of environmental variability, reservoir ecology and human behaviour in shaping disease dynamics [5]. These findings support a practical One Health implication: rodent monitoring should not be treated solely as ecolog- ical research, but as part of an integrated risk-assessment system linking animal, environmental and human health data. papers.title: Human Orthohantavirus infections: From virology and clinical epidemiology to oral biological features and dental practice
papers.abstract: Abstract Hantaviruses are rodent-borne zoonotic pathogens responsible for 2 severe clinical syndromes in humans: hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), affecting an estimated 150,000 to 200,000 individuals annually worldwide, and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), characterized by fulminant pulmonary edema with case fatality rates approaching 40%. Although the systemic manifestations of hantavirus disease are well described, the oral and salivary dimensions of infection have received comparatively little attention in the dental literature. This review synthesizes current evidence on the virology, global epidemiology, pathogenesis, clinical manifestations, oral complications, diagnostic approaches, treatment options, and dental practice implications of human hantavirus infections. A narrative review with a structured search of PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar was conducted, supplemented by hand-searching and by consultation of the World Health Organization and European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control outbreak reporting. Particular attention was directed toward primary research on salivary immunity, oral fluid diagnostics, and salivary gland tropism. Andes virus (ANDV) antigen has been detected in secretory cells of human salivary glands, and ANDV uniquely resists the antiviral capacity of human saliva, providing a biologically plausible mechanism for its person-to-person transmissibility. Infectious virus has since been recovered from saliva and gingival crevicular fluid during acute infection, although a salivary route of transmission remains an epidemiological association rather than proven. In a cohort of 69 confirmed ANDV-infected cases, salivary secretory immunoglobulin A (sIgA) was significantly elevated (4.846 vs. 0.333 mg/mL in exposed-uninfected contacts), whereas mucins MUC7 and MUC5B were more frequently detected in exposed-but-not-infected household contacts, a cross-sectional finding whose direction of causation is unresolved. Total salivary sIgA is a non-specific marker of mucosal immune activation and has no pathogen specificity. Oral fluid IgM assays for Hantaan virus achieved 96.7% sensitivity and 94.9% specificity against serum reference, supporting further evaluation of non-invasive salivary surveillance. Clinically, severe sore throat persisting for 2 to 3 weeks and oropharyngeal edema are documented as early features of hantavirus infection. Thrombocytopenia, which may be profound during the oliguric phase of HFRS, confers significant oral hemorrhagic risk. Human hantavirus infection presents with clinically significant oral and salivary manifestations that are directly relevant to dental practitioners. Dental teams should be aware of the hemorrhagic risk in patients with thrombocytopenia, the aerosol risk in patients with HCPS, the theoretical risk of ANDV transmission via oral contact in endemic regions, and the emerging utility of salivary diagnostics. Recommendations for dental practice are extrapolated from medical, virological, and general infection control evidence, rather than from dental clinical research, and are identified as precautionary where that is the case.

analysis.background: Hantaviruses are rodent‑borne zoonotic pathogens causing hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (150,000‑200,000 cases annually) and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome with case‑fatality rates up to 40%, yet oral and salivary aspects are under‑studied.
analysis.methods: A narrative review was conducted with a structured search of PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, Google Scholar, and supplemental hand‑searching of WHO and ECDC outbreak reports.
analysis.results: ANDV antigen was detected in human salivary‑gland secretory cells and infectious virus recovered from saliva and gingival crevicular fluid; salivary sIgA was markedly elevated in 69 confirmed ANDV cases (4.846 mg/mL vs 0.333 mg/mL in exposed‑uninfected contacts); oral‑fluid IgM assays for Hantaan virus achieved 96.7% sensitivity and 94.9% specificity.
analysis.contribution: The review identifies oral manifestations, hemorrhagic and aerosol risks relevant to dental practice, and demonstrates the promise of salivary diagnostics for non‑invasive surveillance.
analysis.limitations: Recommendations are extrapolated from non‑dental evidence and are precautionary; the work is an abstract‑only narrative review lacking primary dental research.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses cause severe HFRS and HCPS with high morbidity and mortality, but oral aspects are understudied. Methods: A narrative review used a structured search of major biomedical databases and WHO/ECDC reports. Results: ANDV antigen was found in salivary glands, infectious virus recovered from saliva, sIgA was elevated (4.846 vs 0.333 mg/mL) in 69 cases, and oral‑fluid IgM testing showed 96.7% sensitivity and 94.9% specificity. Contribution: Highlights oral risks for dental care and the potential of salivary diagnostics for surveillance. Limitations: Recommendations are precautionary, based on extrapolated evidence, and the article is an abstract‑only review without primary dental data.

papers.title_zh: 人类 正汉坦病毒 感染:从病毒学和临床流行病学到口腔生物特征与牙科实践

analysis_zh.background: 汉坦病毒es是啮齿动物传播的动物源性病原体,导致肾综合征出血热(每年150,000‐200,000例)和汉坦病毒心肺综合征,致死率最高可达40%,但口腔和唾液方面的研究仍不足。
analysis_zh.methods: 进行了一项叙述性综述,采用结构化检索PubMed/MEDLINE、Scopus、Web of Science、Google Scholar,并补充手工检索WHO和ECDC的疫情报告。
analysis_zh.results: 在人体唾液腺分泌细胞中检测到ANDV抗原,并从唾液和牙龈沟液中分离出传染性病毒;在69例确诊的ANDV病例中,唾液sIgA显著升高(4.846 mg/mL 对比 0.333 mg/mL 于暴露未感染接触者);针对汉滩病毒的口腔液IgM检测实现了96.7%的灵敏度和94.9%的特异性。
analysis_zh.contribution: 本综述识别了口腔表现、出血及气溶胶风险,这些与牙科实践相关,并展示了唾液诊断用于非侵入性监测的前景。
analysis_zh.limitations: 建议基于非牙科证据进行推断,属预防性;该工作仅为摘要级叙述性综述,缺乏原始牙科研究。

papers.title: Multi-host circulation and evolutionary dynamics of hantaviruses in small mammals in Southwestern China
papers.abstract: China represents a major hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS)-endemic region, where small mammals, particularly rodents, constitute the principal reservoir hosts. This study characterized HV diversity, RNA detection rate, host range, evolutionary history, and tissue distribution in 1 717 wild small mammals collected from Yunnan Province, China. HVs were detected in 47 animals, corresponding to an overall RNA detection rate of 2.74% (47/1 717, 95% CI: 1.97%–3.51%). At least five HV species or lineages were identified across 10 small mammal species, including Orthohantavirus luxiense (LUXV), Orthohantavirus fugongense (FUGV), Orthohantavirus seoulense (SEOV), Orthohantavirus caobangense (CBNV), and Thottimvirus sp. Host‐virus coevolutionary analysis suggested extensive interspecies transmission, with particularly strong support for phylogenetically inferred host‐switching events involving SEOV and FUGV. Preliminary analysis of tissue viral loads revealed that LUXV was widely distributed across various tissues and that significant differences in viral levels existed among tissues (χ2 = 27.500, P < 0.001). Collectively, these findings elucidate the genetic diversity and evolutionary dynamics of HVs in small mammals in Yunnan.

papers.title_zh: 中国西南地区小型哺乳动物中汉坦病毒es的多宿主循环与进化动态

analysis_zh.background: 中国是主要的肾综合征出血热流行区,主要的宿主是小型哺乳动物,尤其是啮齿类。
analysis_zh.methods: 本研究在中国云南省采集了1,717只野生小型哺乳动物,并对[ PDI0109 ](汉坦病毒)多样性、RNA 检测率、宿主范围、进化历史和组织分布进行了表征。
analysis_zh.results: 在47只动物中检测到汉坦病毒,整体 RNA 检测率为 2.74%(95% 置信区间:1.97%–3.51%)。在10种小型哺乳动物中识别出五种汉坦病毒种类或谱系(LUXV、FUGV、SEOV、CBNV 和 Thottimvirus sp.),其中 LUXV 在组织中分布广泛,且不同组织间病毒负荷差异显著(χ2 = 27.500,P < 0.001)。
analysis_zh.contribution: 宿主-病毒共进化分析揭示了广泛的跨物种传播,并强有力地证实了 SEOV 与 FUGV 之间的宿主转移事件,阐明了云南地区汉坦病毒的遗传多样性和进化动力学。
analysis_zh.limitations: 未在提供的证据中报告。

papers.title: Transmission timing and containment risk in human Andes virus outbreaks
papers.abstract: The 2026 multinational Andes virus (ANDV) outbreak linked to cruise-ship travel from Argentina triggered extensive contact tracing and quarantine. Whether intervention on this scale was necessary or sufficient depends on the risk of onward transmission, which can be difficult to estimate early in an outbreak. Using transmission-pair data from the 2018–2019 outbreak in Epuyén, Argentina, and a mechanistic model linking viral growth, symptom onset, and transmission, we estimated that 42.4% (95% CrI: 18.2–69.7%) of transmission occurs before symptom onset and that the median incubation period is 18.5 days (95% CrI: 16.5–19.5). We simulated outbreaks under an Epuyén-calibrated estimate (R = 2.12, k = 0.316) and a pooled estimate from 15 prior ANDV investigations (R = 0.24, k = 0.39), with intervention beginning after two generations, as in the cruise-associated event. Under the higher-transmission scenario, missing 10% of exposed individuals or downstream contacts resulted in a 29.9% probability of continued spread and a 20.6% probability that at least 5,000 ultimately uninfected people would be quarantined. Under lower transmission, continued spread stayed below 8%. However, the risk of onward transmission could not be estimated precisely from the first several detected cases. These findings therefore support rapid, comprehensive contact tracing and quarantine after large international exposure events despite substantial costs.

Introduction Andes virus (ANDV) is the only hantavirus known to be capable of person-to-person transmission, although documented transmission has been confined to a small number of localized outbreaks [1– 3]. ANDV infection is associated with a case-fatality rate of approximately 36% [4], and there are currently no approved vaccines or specific antiviral therapies. Recent increases in ANDV activity in South America have heightened concern about the potential for person-to-person spread [5]. In 2026, a multinational ANDV exposure event linked to cruise-ship travel from Argentina led to 13 reported cases and 3 deaths, and prompted extensive international contact tracing and prolonged quarantine of 147 passengers and crew from 23 countries [6, 7]. The severity of ANDV disease and its potential for person-to-person spread may warrant such intensive responses, but evidence on their effectiveness and associated quarantine burden remains limited. Evaluating containment strategies requires a detailed understanding of ANDV transmission dy- namics. Decisions about the scale and duration of contact tracing and quarantine depend on incu- bation periods, the timing of infectiousness relative to symptom onset, and individual-level variation in transmission. Long incubation periods prolong monitoring and quarantine, transmission before symptom onset allows infected individuals to spread infection before they are recognized and iso- lated, and variation in transmission means that a small number of infected individuals may account for a disproportionate share of secondary infections. However, estimating these quantities from outbreak data is complicated by evolving control measures, including case detection, isolation, and quarantine, which alter transmission opportunities over time. The 2018–2019 Epuyén outbreak provides the most detailed empirical data on person-to-person ANDV transmission. The original outbreak investigation reconstructed transmission chains, identi- fied superspreading, and estimated that the effective reproduction number (Re) declined from 2.12 before implementation of isolation and quarantine to 0.96 afterward [13]. Most reported ANDV infections, by contrast, arise from zoonotic spillover and are not followed by sustained person-to- person transmission. Transmission in Epuyén concentrated at a birthday party and a wake, in a town of fewer than 2,000 people, suggesting that what distinguishes these outcomes is not where infection is acquired but the number and intensity of close contacts during the brief window around symptom onset, variation in infectiousness across individuals, or both. The relative contributions of contact and infectiousness cannot be resolved from existing investigations, which report secondary cases but not contacts that did not result in transmission. Because incubation can last several weeks, the setting an infected person occupies during the transmission window may differ substan- tially from the setting in which exposure occurred. Transmission potential can therefore vary among cases, locations, and generations of the same outbreak. More recently, a latent-time analysis of the Epuyén transmission-pair data jointly estimated unobserved infection times, generation intervals, transmission timing relative to source symptom onset, time-varying reproduction numbers, and offspring dispersion from interval-censored data [12]. However, it modeled incubation and transmission timing as separate empirical delay distributions rather than as outcomes of a shared within-host process. This limited its ability to represent 2 . Here, we extend the latent-time framework by integrating a mechanistic model that jointly links infection, symptom onset, and transmission [15]. We incorporate the resulting estimates in stochastic branching-process simulations of a multinational exposure event based on the initial timing and magnitude of the 2026 cruise-associated outbreak. Given the variation in transmission observed across past ANDV events, we simulate outbreaks in both high- and low-transmission settings. The high-transmission setting uses parameters estimated from the Epuyén investigation, whereas the low-transmission setting uses pooled estimates from 15 prior ANDV investigations. We estimate the level of contact tracing and quarantine required for containment and quantify the consequences of incomplete or delayed intervention. Results We fitted the within-host-informed latent-time model to 34 cases and 33 reconstructed source- recipient pairs from the 2018–2019 Epuyén outbreak in Argentina (Table 1; Figure 1). Transmission was concentrated near source symptom onset, with an estimated 42.4% of transmission events oc- curring before symptoms appeared (95% CrI: 18.2–69.7%). The median transmission time was 0.07 days after source symptom onset (95% CrI: (-0.20) to 0.30 days), and the central 95% of transmission events occurred from 0.85 days before to 2.02 days after source symptom onset (Figure 1A). The median incubation period was 18.50 days (95% CrI: 16.50–19.50 days), with a central 95% distributional interval of 7.50–35.50 days (Figure 1C). An estimated 95% of infections developed symptoms by 31.50 days (95% CrI: 29.50–35.50), and 99% by 39.50 days (95% CrI: 35.50–44.50). The median generation interval was 22.50 days (95% CrI: 20.50–23.50 days) (Figure 1B), and the median serial interval was 21.79 days (95% CrI: 21.28–22.18 days) (Figure 1D). Thus, exposed individuals may require several weeks of follow-up even though onward transmission is concentrated within a narrow window around symptom onset. These estimates were broadly consistent with previous analyses of the Epuyén outbreak while providing model-based inference of latent infection times and transmission timing relative to symptom onset (Supplementary Results). The central 95% interval summarizes the expected range across individual infections or transmission events. Transmission timing is reported relative to source symptom onset, with negative values indicating transmission before symptom onset. Solid curves represent posterior median densities, and shaded regions indicate the corresponding 95% credible intervals. Dashed vertical lines mark zero days. In panel A, negative values indicate transmission before source symptom onset; in panel D, negative values indicate that the recipient developed symptoms before the source case. To characterize the transmission conditions documented across settings, we analyzed 15 pub- lished ANDV investigations. A hierarchical negative-binomial model estimated a pooled reproduc- tion number of 0.24 (95% CrI: 0.12–0.48) and a shared dispersion parameter of 0.39 (95% CrI: 0.19–0.89), reflecting low average but highly variable realized transmission across this broader set of investigations. Together with the Epuyén-calibrated estimates (R=2.12, k=0.316), these results anchored an empirically informed range of ANDV transmission potential. Hereafter, we refer to simulations using the Epuyén and pooled parameterizations as the higher- and lower-transmission scenarios, respectively. The primary analysis reproduced the timing of the 2026 cruise-associated response, with inter- vention beginning on simulation day 35, 26 days after symptom onset in the first detected case. 4 . Tracing failures had substantially greater consequences under higher transmission (Figure 2A). When tracing missed 5%, 10%, 25%, or 50% of exposed individuals or downstream contacts, post-response transmission outside quarantine occurred in 18.9%, 29.9%, 51.1%, and 70.8% of simulations, respectively. Under the lower transmission, this probability ranged from 0.7% with 5% missed to 7.8% with 50% missed. Among simulations with higher transmission and at least one additional post-response infection, missing 10% of contacts resulted in a median of 5 additional infections and a 95th percentile of 49. With 25% or 50% missed, the medians increased to 8 and 27, respectively, and the 95th percentiles to 111 and 351. With lower transmission, the median remained between one and two across tracing levels (Figure 2B). Quarantine burdens were substantially lower under lower transmission (Figure 2C). With 10% of contacts missed, the median number of retrospectively uninfected downstream contacts quaran- tined was 313 (IQR 185–440), compared with 1,821 (IQR 720–4,161) under the higher-transmission scenario. At lower transmission, the median burden fell by 49%, from 329 with complete tracing to 167 with 50% of contacts missed, because outbreaks were small and fewer contacts were traced. At higher transmission, fewer quarantines per case were offset by larger outbreaks and more tracing events, leaving the median comparatively stable but increasing the risk of very large quarantine burdens. Most response activity ended within the initial six-week quarantine period, but breakthrough transmission occasionally prolonged the response under the higher-transmission scenario. With 10% of contacts missed, the median additional response duration was zero months, the 95th percentile was 1.61 months, and 0.2% of simulations required at least four additional months of response activity. With 50% missed, the median increased to 1.02 months and the 95th percentile to 5.01 months. With lower transmission, additional response duration remained near zero (Figure 2D). The multinational response to the 2026 cruise-associated outbreak was initiated after seven confirmed or suspected cases were identified. To assess the consequences of delayed intervention, we initiated contact tracing and quarantine after different numbers of cases had been reported, assuming 95% tracing completeness (Figure 3). Under higher transmission, delaying intervention from the first to the twentieth reported case increased the probability of at least 100 infections from 2.7% to 38.2% and of at least 500 infections from 2.1% to 14.0%. Median outbreak size increased from 1 to 72 infections, median quarantine burden from 2 to 500 individuals, and the probability of quarantining at least 1,000 individuals from 2.7% to 36.0%. Under lower transmission, outbreaks rarely reached the later intervention points: only 13 of 10,000 simulations reached 10 reported cases, and none reached 20. Outcomes following greater delays therefore could not be estimated precisely. Under active containment, most simulated outbreaks ended before enough cases were detected to estimate the reproduction number precisely. Estimates from the first few detected cases were highly uncertain, with broad 95% credible intervals that commonly included R = 1 under both transmission scenarios (Supplementary Figure 5). papers.title: Andes virus from the MV Hondius outbreak is highly pathogenic in hamsters and airborne shed
papers.abstract: In May 2026, an outbreak of hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) caused by Andes virus (ANDV) was detected aboard the cruise ship MV Hondius, sparking public health measures in multiple countries. ANDV infections in humans are mostly sporadic, most often linked to exposure to infected rodents in South America, although small clusters of human cases, like the 2026 outbreak on the MV Hondius occur as well. It is not known whether virological factors may contribute to this distinct epidemiology, and no phenotypic characterisation of the newly emerged ANDV (ANDV2026) has been carried out to date. Here, using an ANDV isolate from a presymptomatic patient from the MV Hondius, we studied pathogenesis, identified sites of viral replication, characterized innate and adaptive immune responses, and quantified shedding in golden Syrian hamsters. ANDV2026 proved to be highly pathogenic in hamsters, causing severe pulmonary disease reminiscent of HPS. ANDV2026 triggered a delayed type-I IFN response and inflammatory response in the lungs consistent with the key pathological features of HPS, and we detected viral replication in both respiratory and extra-respiratory tissues, including the brain. Infected animals mounted neutralising antibodies and T cell responses, the latter directed predominantly against the L and N proteins. Importantly, ANDV2026-infected animals shed virus through multiple routes, and we detected infectious virus in air samplers connected to cages housing ANDV2026-infected hamsters. In contrast, control hamsters infected with a rodent-derived ANDV isolate (ANDV9717869) shed little virus and air samples were consistently negative. These findings consolidate established features of ANDV pathogenesis, while revealing properties not previously described. Phenotypic characterisation of patient-derived ANDV isolates in animal models can strengthen outbreak preparedness, identify markers of disease severity, and support the development of medical countermeasures.

ANDV infections in humans are mostly sporadic, most often linked to exposure 27 to infected rodents in South America, although small clusters of human cases, like the 2026 28 outbreak on the MV Hondius occur as well. It is not known whether virological factors may 29 contribute to this distinct epidemiology, and no phenotypic characterization of the newly emerged 30 ANDV (ANDV2026) has been carried out to date. Here, using an ANDV isolate from a 31 presymptomatic patient from the MV Hondius, we studied pathogenesis, identified sites of viral 32 replication, characterized innate and adaptive immune responses, and quantified shedding in 33 golden Syrian hamsters. ANDV2026 proved to be highly pathogenic in hamsters, causing severe 34 pulmonary disease reminiscent of HPS. ANDV2026 triggered a delayed type-I IFN response and 35 inflammatory response in the lungs consistent with the key pathological features of HPS, and we 36 detected viral replication in both respiratory and extra-respiratory tissues, including the brain. 37 Infected animals mounted neutralizing antibodies and T cell responses, the latter directed 38 predominantly against the L and N proteins. Importantly, ANDV2026-infected animals shed virus 39 through multiple routes, and we detected infectious virus in air samplers connected to cages 40 housing ANDV2026-infected hamsters. In contrast, control hamsters infected with a rodent-derived 41 ANDV isolate (ANDV9717869) shed little virus and air samples were consistently negative. These 42 findings consolidate established features of ANDV pathogenesis, while revealing properties not 43 previously described. Phenotypic characterization of patient-derived ANDV isolates in animal 44 models can strengthen outbreak preparedness, identify markers of disease severity, and support 45 the development of medical countermeasures. 46 3 | P a g e INTRODUCTION 47 On the 2nd of May 2026, a cluster of severe respiratory disease aboard the Dutch cruise ship MV 48 Hondius was notified to the World Health organization (WHO)1-3. Soon after, ANDV was 49 diagnosed as the cause of the outbreak, which overall led to 13 reported cases, including three 50 deaths4. Confirmed cases were all aboard the MV Hondius, although the outbreak led to 51 monitoring of 653 individuals in 33 countries around the globe. 52 ANDV is classified within the family Orthohantaviridae5-8. These are viruses that cause two distinct 53 disease complexes: the hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) in Europe and Asia, and 54 the hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) in the Americas, caused among others by Sin Nombre 55 virus (SNV) and Andes virus (ANDV), respectively9. HPS is usually presents in four distinct clinical 56 phases: febrile, cardiopulmonary, diuretic and convalescent10,11. Most cases are characterized by 57 pulmonary edema driven by increased vascular permeability, terminally leading to cardiogenic 58 shock and death12. The case fatality rate of the MV Hondius outbreak was 23%, lower than for 59 previously reported ANDV clusters. Direct comparison is difficult however, due to the relatively 60 low number of cases in this outbreak and early access to medical care for many of the individuals 61 affected13-15. 62 ANDV is endemic in Southern Argentina and Chile, where it causes seasonal outbreaks every 63 year9,16. Humans are believed to become infected mostly after exposure to aerosolized infectious 64 excretions of the rodent reservoir, the long-tailed rice rat (Oligoryzomys longicaudatus)5,6,17. 65 Andes virus (ANDV) was first detected in 1995, when it caused an outbreak of 16 cases and nine 66 deaths18. This outbreak and subsequent ones suggested that ANDV can be capable of human- 67 to-human transmission, with the main risk factor being in close contact with infected individuals in 68 enclosed settings18,19. Some cases have also been described without any documented direct 69 contact, hinting at a respiratory transmission route, though available data cannot distinguish 70 airborne shedding of infectious virus from contamination of the surrounding environment20. On 71 the MV Hondius, patients were in direct contact with each other, suggesting ANDV human-to- 72 4 | P a g e human transmission. One potential asymptomatic case of ANDV infection in a health-care worker 73 with low-level viraemia was also reported, despite only indirect exposure21-23. 74 Few studies have phenotyped ANDV isolates obtained directly from human patients21-23, and 75 fewer still have done so in vivo to define key viral characteristics such as virulence and host 76 responses22,24. This reflects the sporadic nature of HPS and its restricted geographical distribution. 77 ANDV is also notoriously difficult to isolate, as infection is typically diagnosed once patients have 78 already developed neutralizing antibodies. As a result, our understanding of the biological 79 differences between ANDV isolates associated with different cases and outbreaks is incomplete. 80 Here, we characterized the ANDV isolate associated with the MV Hondius outbreak 81 (ANDV/2026/hondius-NL-12, henceforth ANDV2026). Using the golden Syrian hamster model, we 82 studied viral pathogenesis, replication sites, and the host innate and adaptive immune responses. 83 We also analyzed virus shedding from infected animals and sampled air from the cages of infected 84 hamsters for ANDV RNA and infectious virus. Throughout our study, the human isolate ANDV2026 85 was compared with a rodent-derived ANDV strain (ANDV9717869). Altogether, in vivo phenotyping 86 contributes to the continuous risk assessment of emerging viruses of global health concern. 87 88 RESULTS 89 90 ANDV2026 causes severe, systemic infection in hamsters. Golden Syrian hamsters were 91 intranasally inoculated with a low dose (200 TCID50/hamster) of either ANDV2026 (n=18) or 92 ANDV9717869 (n=18). ANDV2026 was isolated from whole-blood sample collected from a pre- 93 symptomatic patient during the 2026 ANDV outbreak linked to the cruise ship MV Hondius3. 94 Backtitration of the inocula revealed that the animals received a dose of 28 TCID50 of ANDV2026 95 and 89 TCID50 of ANDV9717869. Six animals per group were sacrificed at 3, 7 and 14 days post- 96 inoculation (dpi), or earlier when reaching humane endpoints. Sixty percent of the hamsters 97 inoculated with ANDV2026 reached the humane endpoint between 12 and 14 dpi (Fig 1a). 98 5 | P a g e Symptoms included lethargy, ruffled fur, decreased mobility, and severe respiratory distress. In 99 general, animals reached humane endpoints within 24-72 hours after the onset of symptoms. The 100 development of clinical symptoms was also accompanied by a loss of body weight of up to 9% in 101 three days (Fig. 1b). At the terminal stage of the experiment (12-14 dpi), the lung-to-bodyweight 102 ratio of ANDV2026 inoculated animals was significantly increased when compared to both mock- 103 and ANDV9717869-inoculated animals (Fig. 1c). These values reflected the macroscopic lung 104 lesions observed in ANDV2026 inoculated animals, characterized by increased size, rounded edges 105 and darkened color with severe, diffuse lung oedema (Fig. 1d), as described previously for severe 106 ANDV infections in hamsters25-27. 107 Next, we tested 15 respiratory and non-respiratory tissues for presence of both viral RNA by qRT- 108 PCR and infectious virus by titration (Fig. 1e,f). At the early timepoints (3 dpi), viral RNA and 109 infectious virus were only detected in the nasal turbinates with titers essentially identical in both 110 ANDV2026- and ANDV9717869-inoculated animals. At 7 and 12-14 dpi all tissues contained both viral 111 RNA and infectious virus with titers in most cases higher in ANDV2026-infected animals. 112 Interestingly, we observed no significant differences in viral loads in myocardium and liver 113 between ANDV2026- and ANDV9717869-infected hamsters 12-14 dpi. These tissues were previously 114 reported as the prime targets of virus replication in ANDV9717869-infected hamsters26. We observed 115 the highest viral titers in the respiratory tract (nasal turbinates and lungs), submandibular salivary 116 glands, pancreas, and adrenal glands collected from ANDV2026-infected animals. 117 Sites of ANDV replication. Next, we investigated the sites of viral replication using 118 immunohistochemistry (IHC) and RNA in situ-hybridisation (ISH) in formalin-fixed and paraffin 119 embedded samples from inoculated animals. In the lungs, we detected abundant viral RNA (Fig. 120 2a) and protein in ANDV2026-infected animals at 7dpi, with widespread distribution in the 121 parenchyma. Quantification of RNA signal showed virus spread in wider areas of the lungs in 122 ANDV2026-infected hamsters compared to those infected with ANDV9717869 (Fig. 2b-c), both at 7 123 and 14 dpi. Virus RNA was detectable, both by qualitative assessment of the histological sections 124 6 | P a g e and by software-assisted image analysis28, in the lung parenchyma and endothelial cells, but not 125 in the bronchial epithelium of all ANDV infected animals at both 7 and 14 dpi (Fig. 2c-d). As 126 expected, extrarespiratory organs such as liver, kidney, myocardium, and many others showed 127 abundant viral RNA signal in endothelial cells, while epithelial cells were viral RNA negative (Fig. 128 2e). Importantly, we also detected ANDV2026 widely distributed in the brain, including in endothelial 129 cells of blood vessels, meninges and neurons (Fig. 2e and Fig. S1). 130 The widespread infection of endothelial cells throughout all organs was not accompanied by 131 severe histopathological lesions in both groups of animals. Serum chemistry revealed reduced 132 total protein and albumin concentrations in ANDV2026-infected hamsters compared to ANDV9717869- 133 and mock-infected animals, consistent with endothelial dysfunction and leakage of proteins to the 134 extravascular space (Fig. 2f). We found moderately abnormal values for alkaline phosphatase, 135 alanine-aminotransferase, blood urea nitrogen, creatinine and phosphorus in ANDV2026-infected 136 animals (in the terminal stages of the disease), consistent with kidney and liver damage, although 137 major histopathological lesions were not observed (Fig. 2f, Fig. S2). Serum values of amylase, 138 calcium, glucose, sodium and total bilirubin remained similar between groups (Fig. S2). 139 Lung pathology in ANDV2026-infected hamsters correlates with preferential activation of the 140 type I IFN response. At the latest stages of disease, we detected histopathological lesions 141 throughout the lungs in hamsters infected with ANDV2026, similar to severe HPS previously 142 described in this model 25-27. Lesions include diffuse alveolar damage, multifocal, 143 lymphoplasmacytic infiltration, alveolar histiocytosis, alveolar oedema, leukocytolastic vasculitis, 144 perivascular oedema, sloughing of bronchial epithelial cells to various degrees and hemorrhages 145 in the vessel (Fig. 3a-b). We also detected fibrin accumulation in damaged alveoli in more severe 146 cases (Fig. 3b, middle panel). Infiltrates of both B-cells (Pax+ cells) and macrophage (Iba-1+ cells) 147 infiltrates, but not T-cells (CD3+), were observed in the lungs of ANDV2026-infected animals (Fig. 148 3c-d). 149 7 | P a g e In addition, activation of the type I IFN response (henceforth IFN), assessed by the upregulation 150 of the IFN-stimulated gene Mx-1, was evident in the lungs of both ANDV2026- and ANDV9217869- 151 infected animals (Fig. 3d, last column). We detected relatively little Mx-1 at 7 dpi despite the 152 presence of abundant virus replication. This observation reinforces the concept that ANDV is able 153 to evade recognition by the host IFN response for some time. 154 Because ANDV, both in humans and in hamsters, causes primarily a pulmonary disease, we 155 further investigated whether the levels of the IFN response vary between lungs and other organs 156 (Fig. 4). To this end, we quantified the expression of IFIT-1 RNA, another interferon stimulated 157 gene (ISG), in FFPE sections of lungs, spleen, myocardium, kidney and liver of ANDV2026-infected 158 animals by RNAscope and normalized the data in relation to the presence of viral RNA in each of 159 these organs. We found the highest relative expression of IFIT-1 RNA in the lungs, followed by 160 the spleen (Fig. 4). These data are in line with the relatively upregulation of proinflammatory 161 genes such as CXCL10 that we detected in these two organs (Fig. S3). Of note, we did find 162 bronchial epithelial cells expressing ISGs in the absence of viral replication (Fig. 4a), most likely 163 triggered by an IFN response in infected neighboring cells. The IFN and inflammatory response 164 in respiratory epithelia may explain the lesions (sloughed off cells) observed in some of these 165 animals. 166 Combined, ANDV2026 causes a disease comparable to HPS in hamsters, characterized 167 predominantly by lung pathology, endothelial cell dysfunction, with a relatively long incubation 168 period where abundant virus replication does not trigger a detectable inflammatory response. 169 Adaptive immune response to ANDV in experimentally inoculated hamsters. We next 170 assessed antibody and T-cell responses in ANDV-infected animals. We detected neutralizing 171 antibodies only at 12-14 dpi in sera from animals infected with either ANDV9717869 or ANDV2026. 172 The mean VNT50 did not differ significantly between groups, even though all ANDV2026-infected 173 animals mounted a response compared to 40% of the ANDV9717689-infected animals (Fig. 5a). To 174 further characterize the ANDV-specific adaptive immune response, we isolated lymphocytes from 175 8 | P a g e hamster lungs at both 7 and 14 dpi and stimulated them with overlapping peptide pools covering 176 the N, Gn, Gc, and L proteins (the latter split in four distinct pools, L1-4) (Fig. 5b). At 7 dpi, antigen- 177 specific T-cell responses were limited in all groups (Fig. 5d). However, strong antigen-specific T- 178 cell responses were detected at 12-14 dpi regardless of group. The majority of virus-specific T- 179 cells targeted the L-protein (Fig. 5c, Fig. S4); these were comparable between ANDV9717869- and 180 ANDV2026-inoculated hamsters, and higher than those observed in mock-inoculated animals, 181 although significance was reached only for ANDV9717869 (Fig. 5e). N-specific T-cell responses 182 were higher in ANDV9717869-inoculated animals than in ANDV2026- and mock-inoculated animals at 183 12-14 dpi (Fig. 5e). Similar responses were observed with lymphocytes isolated from the spleen, 184 although the background in mock-inoculated hamsters was higher, complicating data 185 interpretation (Fig. S4). 186 Infectious virus is shed in the air by ANDV2026-infected animals. The ANDV outbreak aboard 187 the MV Hondius raised questions about the potential of increased shedding, and hence increased 188 transmissibility, of ANDV. In hamsters, we detected viral genomes (Fig. 6a) and infectious virus 189 (Fig. S5) in throat swabs of all ANDV2026-inoculated animals from 7 dpi onwards, with 190 progressively increasing titers until the end of the experiment (Fig. 6a). We detected infectious 191 virus in only one ANDV9717869-infected animal. By immunohistochemistry, we detected numerous 192 clusters of ANDV2026 infected endothelial cells, olfactory epithelium, degenerated and sloughing 193 olfactory epithelium, as well as the ducts of the nasal submucosal glands of the olfactory portion 194 of the turbinates, especially at 14 dpi. Only very few cells of the respiratory epithelium showed 195 occasionally virus positive signal (Fig. 6d-f). ANDV9717869-inoculated animals displayed only 196 occasional virus-positive cells in the nasal turbinates (either endothelial cells, cells within the 197 olfactory epithelium, or the submucosal glands). 198 We also detected ANDV2026 RNA in urine collected at study endpoints, but volumes were too small 199 to test for presence of infectious virus. Furthermore, we detected both viral RNA and infectious 200 9 | P a g e virus in feces homogenates collected from cages housing ANDV2026 infected animals (Fig. 6c and 201 S5). 202 Hence, ANDV2026-infected animals shed infectious virus from the respirat…
